items.physical_scope: Conditional model statements about a uniformly accelerated ideal observer in flat classical special relativity: the domain of the Rindler chart, the causal past and future boundaries (horizons) of the congruence worldlines, and the radar time and distance assigned to coaxial congruence worldlines by ideal light signals and ideal clocks. Excludes gravitation, media and dispersion, real apparatus, finite resolution, quantum fields and the Unruh effect, and material models of guide or reflector; no measurement, statistical or empirical claim is made.

items.title: The guided-ring Sagnac delay: return times and receiver proper-time difference for counter-propagating guided signals on a rotating ring
items.statement: Adopt post-sr-inertial-covariance and post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light and the SI conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions (x^0 = c t). Let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart). Fix R > 0, a real Omega with |Omega| R < c, a real x^3_0 and a real phi_0, and put gamma := (1 - Omega^2 R^2/c^2)^{-1/2}. A rigidly rotating circular ring of radius R and height x^3_0 about the x^3-axis, with angular velocity Omega, has material worldlines W_{phi_0}(t) := x^{-1}(c t, R cos(phi_0 + Omega t), R sin(phi_0 + Omega t), x^3_0), t in R. (i) The ring worldline and the ring congruence. W_{phi_0} is a C^infinity future timelike worldline with unit observer n = gamma (1, -(Omega R/c) sin(phi_0+Omega t), (Omega R/c) cos(phi_0+Omega t), 0) = (gamma/c) partial_t|_{varphi}, eta(n,n) = -1, and four-velocity U = c n = c gamma (1, -(Omega R/c) sin(phi_0+Omega t), (Omega R/c) cos(phi_0+Omega t), 0) = gamma partial_t|_{varphi}, eta(U,U) = -c^2, where varphi := phi - Omega t is the rotating angular label of the ring material points; it is an unparametrized flow line of the rigid-rotation congruence n = gamma(r) [partial_0 + (Omega/c)(-x^2 partial_1 + x^1 partial_2)] restricted to r = R, and its proper time tau and the chart time t satisfy d tau = dt/gamma, so tau = t/gamma + tau_0 for an arbitrary proper-time origin tau_0 on this worldline (thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples (c), def-sr-proper-time, lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization). (ii) The guided-signal model. Adopt, as an explicit model assumption of an ideal circular guide attached to the ring and of the signal and detector model below, and not as a consequence of the postulates: two ideal signals are emitted at the common emission event W_{phi_0}(0) into the guide, one in the positive angular direction and one in the negative angular direction (respectively co-rotating and counter-rotating for Omega > 0, with these roles reversed for Omega < 0), and in the inertial chart they follow the curves C_+ and C_- given by phi_+(t) = phi_0 + c t/R and phi_-(t) = phi_0 - c t/R with radius R and height x^3_0, i.e. each guided signal has chart angular rate +c/R or -c/R along the guide ('inertial tangential speed c along the guide'); the detector is an ideal clock carried by the ring material point labelled varphi = phi_0. Each of C_+ and C_- is a future null curve of the chart: its tangent has time component c and spatial part of Euclidean length c, so the tangent has eta-norm 0 and positive time component (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets). (iii) Return times and differences. The displayed guided curves have all-real mathematical extensions; emitted signals are their restrictions t >= 0. On those extensions C_+ meets the worldline W_{phi_0} exactly at the chart times 2 pi k R/(c - Omega R), k in Z, and C_- exactly at the chart times 2 pi k R/(c + Omega R), k in Z; the smallest positive meeting times are t_1 := 2 pi R/(c - Omega R) > 0 and t_2 := 2 pi R/(c + Omega R) > 0. Hence the two counter-propagating signals emitted at the same event reunite with the emitting material point at the reception events W_{phi_0}(t_1) and W_{phi_0}(t_2), each having gained exactly one circuit relative to that material point, and the chart-time difference of the two reunions is t_1 - t_2 = 4 pi Omega R^2/(c^2 - Omega^2 R^2) > 0 for Omega > 0. The proper-time difference measured by the detector ideal clock is (t_1 - t_2)/gamma = 4 pi Omega R^2/(c^2 sqrt(1 - Omega^2R^2/c^2)). For Omega = 0 (inertial ring) t_1 = t_2 = 2 pi R/c and both differences vanish; for Omega < 0 the sign of the first difference reverses and the roles of C_+ and C_- are interchanged. (iv) Relation to the ring rest-synchronization holonomy. On the fixed-height timelike cylinder C = {r = R, x^3 = x^3_0}, material worldlines have constant rotating label. Its rest lines instead vary varphi on an angular lift and satisfy dt/dvarphi = Omega R^2/(c^2 - Omega^2R^2), being integral curves of partial_varphi + [Omega R^2/(c^2 - Omega^2R^2)] partial_t; for Omega = 0 they are t = constant circles; one circuit varphi -> varphi + 2 pi has the chart-time holonomy Delta t_h = 2 pi Omega R^2/(c^2 - Omega^2R^2) = (t_1 - t_2)/2 and the receiver proper-time holonomy Delta tau_h = Delta t_h/gamma = 2 pi Omega R^2/(c^2 sqrt(1 - Omega^2R^2/c^2)) = (1/2)(t_1 - t_2)/gamma, exactly half of the detector proper-time difference of (iii); for Omega = 0 both holonomies vanish. The ambient three-dimensional rest distribution of the rotating congruence is nowhere integrable for Omega != 0, so no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists, while the one-dimensional rest distribution restricted to the fixed-height cylinder C is locally integrable and has the global holonomy just computed, nonvanishing exactly when Omega != 0; the return-time computation of (iii) uses only the guided null curves and the material worldline and does not use either integrability property (thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples (c), thm-sr-local-congruence-adapted-charts-and-frobenius). (v) Scope. All quantities are conditional model computations for the specified ring, guide, signal and detector idealizations. The guided-signal curves are an adopted device model: the ideal vacuum light rays of post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light are straight future null lines and do not circulate around the ring by themselves, and no assertion is made about optical fibers, refractive media, dispersion, absorption, finite resolution, apparatus calibration, interference phase or wave optics, or about one-way synchronization conventions between distinct ring observers; no measurement outcome, statistical inference or empirical claim is made, the values of R and Omega are parameters and not measured quantities, and no choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Direct computation on the fixed-height timelike cylinder C={r=R,x^3=x^3_0}. (i) Differentiate W with the sine/cosine derivative and chain-rule suppliers to obtain dot W=(c,-Omega R sin phi,Omega R cos phi,0), where phi=phi_0+Omega t. Pythagoras gives eta(dot W,dot W)=-c^2+Omega^2R^2=-c^2/gamma^2<0 and dot W^0=c>0. The exact proper-time and four-velocity suppliers give d tau=dt/gamma, n=(gamma/c)dot W with eta(n,n)=-1, and U=gamma dot W=cn with eta(U,U)=-c^2. Since dot W=partial_t|varphi, n=(gamma/c)partial_t|varphi and U=gamma partial_t|varphi. Parametrization by s=c tau makes the material curve an integral curve of n; chart-time parametrization gives the same unparametrized flow line. (ii) Differentiating the adopted C_+ and C_- curves gives time component c and spatial norm c, hence future null tangents, without deducing the circular guide model from straight vacuum-ray postulates. (iii) The exact trigonometric addition/parity, quarter-turn, and zero-set suppliers show that two sine/cosine pairs agree exactly when their angles differ by 2 pi k: addition gives sin(angle difference)=0 and cos(angle difference)=1; the zero-set result puts the difference in pi Z, and pi shifts negate cosine, leaving only even integers. Thus C_+ meets the material curve when (c/R-Omega)t=2 pi k, while C_- meets it when -(c/R+Omega)t=2 pi k. In the latter relabel m=-k. Both denominators c-Omega R and c+Omega R are positive on |Omega|R<c, so all-real extensions have exactly the stated integer meeting sets, and signals emitted at t=0 have first positive reunion at winding magnitude one. Subtract the two return times to obtain Delta t=4 pi Omega R^2/(c^2-Omega^2R^2), then divide by gamma to obtain the detector proper-time difference. Omega=0 gives equal returns and zero differences; negative Omega interchanges co-/counter-rotation and reverses the signed differences. (iv) The rigid-rotation supplier gives the fixed-height cylinder metric -D dt^2+2 Omega R^2 dt dvarphi+R^2 dvarphi^2, D=c^2-Omega^2R^2>0. Orthogonality to the material tangent partial_t gives -D dt+Omega R^2 dvarphi=0, so rest lines are generated by partial_varphi+(Omega R^2/D)partial_t, not by constant-label material lines. Integration over a positive 2 pi angular lift gives Delta t_h=2 pi Omega R^2/D and the signed receiver offset Delta tau_h=Delta t_h/gamma, exactly half the corresponding signal-return differences. At zero Omega the rest lines close at constant t. The ambient rank-three rest distribution is locally nonintegrable for nonzero Omega by the rigid-rotation/Frobenius suppliers; the cylinder's rank-one rest lines are locally integrable and their nonzero winding offset is a separate global obstruction. (v) All device-model, ideal-clock, no-measurement and empirical-scope qualifications are retained. No choice principle is used.

references.title: Wikipedia, 'Sagnac effect' (encyclopedia article consulted as a secondary treatment): the basic circular case with return times t_1 = 2 pi R/(c - R omega) and t_2 = 2 pi R/(c + R omega) and the time difference Delta t = 4 pi R^2 omega/(c^2 - R^2 omega^2), its small-velocity limit 4 A omega/c^2, and the guided-wave description of a closed optical path

B. Crowell, Special Relativity, revision 2020-12-10 (author-published undergraduate textbook, 246 PDF pages): Sections 8.1.1-8.1.3 pp. 165-166 (no Einstein synchronization in a rotating frame, the synchronization discrepancy accumulating around a closed circuit, and the Sagnac effect of a rotating ring, with the time shift 2 A omega/c^2 and the ring-laser and fiber-gyroscope examples); signature (+---) converted to (-+++), c = 1 formulas restored to x^0 = c t

items.physical_scope: Conditional kinematic computation in flat classical special relativity for an ideal rigidly rotating circular ring, an adopted ideal circular guide carrying two counter-propagating guided signals with inertial tangential speed c, and an ideal clock detector on the ring. The guide and detector models are explicit idealizations, not consequences of the special-relativistic postulates; the item excludes real optical fibers, refractive and dispersive media, apparatus, finite resolution, interference and wave optics, gravitation and quantum effects, and it makes no measurement, statistical or empirical claim and no claim about sending signals between different material points of the ring.

items.title: Bell's rockets and thread: constant chart-frame separation of equal chart-frame accelerations with nonvanishing longitudinal expansion of the translated congruence
items.statement:
Adopt [[post-sr-inertial-covariance]] and the SI conventions $x^0=ct$ of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]] in an inertial chart ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Let $J$ be an open interval containing $0$, let $q:J\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ with $|q\prime(t)|<c$, set $\beta=q\prime/c$ and $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$, let $L>0$, and fix transverse coordinates $(y_0,z_0)$. The rocket and thread-element worldlines are $x_\xi(t)=x^{-1}(ct,q(t)+\xi,y_0,z_0)$, with labels in an open interval $I$ containing $[0,L]$; the rockets are labels $0,L$.
(a) Every member is $C^2$ future timelike: its chart-time tangent is $(c,q\prime,0,0)$ with squared norm $-c^2/\gamma^2<0$. Its common proper-time function is $\tau(t):=\int_0^t\gamma(v)^{-1}dv$, and its proper four-velocity is $U=\gamma(c,q\prime,0,0)$ with squared norm $-c^2$. All members have equal chart velocity and acceleration, $q\prime,q\prime\prime$, and their chart separation is the constant $L$.
(b) The four-dimensional extension is essential for applying the material-family lemma. Choose open transverse intervals $Y,Z$ containing $y_0,z_0$, put $\sigma:=c\tau$, let $t=t(\sigma)$ be the inverse on $c\tau(J)$, and set
$$\Phi(\sigma,\xi,y,z):=x^{-1}(ct(\sigma),q(t(\sigma))+\xi,y,z),\qquad(\xi,y,z)\in B:=I\times Y\times Z.$$
This is an injective $C^2$ immersion onto an open set, with $dt/d\sigma=\gamma/c$ and $\partial_\sigma\Phi=n(\Phi)$, where $n=\gamma(1,\beta,0,0)$ is a $C^1$ future unit field. Apply the first-order definitions in [[lem-sr-connecting-field-stretching]], which agree with [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] when smooth. The longitudinal unit rest vector is $s_\parallel:=\gamma(\beta,1,0,0)$, and
$$\theta(s_\parallel,s_\parallel)=\gamma^3q\prime q\prime\prime/c^3.$$
This agrees with [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]](d), is nonzero exactly where $q\prime q\prime\prime\ne0$, and changes sign with that product. When $q$ is smooth the full original smooth-congruence branch is recovered. Restricting the extension to fixed $y_0,z_0$ gives the prescribed thread.
(c) For its material label tangent $e=\partial_\xi\Phi=(0,1,0,0)$, $h(e,e)=\gamma^2$ and $h(e)/\gamma=s_\parallel$. The vector $e/\gamma$ generally is not $s_\parallel$, but horizontality implies $\theta(e/\gamma,e/\gamma)=\theta(s_\parallel,s_\parallel)$. The internal longitudinal material metric is $G_{11}=\gamma^2$, so its length at common flow parameter is
$$\mathcal L(t):=\int_0^L\sqrt{G_{11}}d\xi=\gamma(t)L.$$
It is an internal material metric length, not automatically the finite endpoint distance on one observer's orthogonal simultaneity hyperplane. The local evolution is
$$\frac{d}{d\tau}\log\mathcal L=c\theta(s_\parallel,s_\parallel)=\gamma^3q\prime q\prime\prime/c^2,\qquad\frac{d\mathcal L}{d\tau}=\gamma^4Lq\prime q\prime\prime/c^2.$$
At a time with $q\prime=v$, $\mathcal L=L/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\ge L$, with equality exactly for $v=0$. Chart separation stays $L$; the material length is constant precisely when $q\prime{}^2$ is constant, and has nonzero local rate wherever $q\prime q\prime\prime\ne0$.
(d) Under the stipulated material reading that thread elements follow these flow lines, the initial internal length is $\gamma(0)L$ and its relative factor is $\gamma(t)/\gamma(0)$. Relative to that initial state it stretches where $\gamma(t)>\gamma(0)$, shrinks where $\gamma(t)<\gamma(0)$, and has equal length where the factors agree. In the special initially resting case $q\prime(0)=0$, the initial length is $L$ and every state with $q\prime(t)\ne0$ has stretch factor $\gamma(t)>1$. No elasticity or failure criterion is supplied, so neither breaking nor a definite tension of an actual thread follows.
(e) The Rindler congruence in [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]](b) is Born rigid, with constant internal rest separations and unequal proper accelerations $c^2/\rho$ at distinct radial labels ([[def-sr-proper-acceleration]]). Equal chart-velocity and acceleration profiles in the translated family do not imply Born rigidity where $q\prime q\prime\prime\ne0$. Constant chart separation and constant internal rest metric are distinct kinematic conditions.
(f) This is a conditional flat-spacetime deduction for prescribed worldlines and the stated material reading. It assumes no dynamical or elastic model, force law, material failure criterion, measurement or empirical fact, and asserts nothing about real threads or rockets. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
(a) Differentiate the given worldlines. The chart-time tangent has norm $-c^2+q\prime{}^2=-c^2/\gamma^2$ and positive time component, so it is nonzero future timelike. Proper time gives $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ and $U=dx/d\tau=\gamma(c,q\prime,0,0)$; its norm is $-c^2$ ([[def-sr-proper-time]], [[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]], [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The separation and equality of chart derivatives follow directly.
(b) Since $q$ is $C^2$, $\gamma$ is $C^1$ and $\tau\prime=1/\gamma$ is positive $C^1$, so $\tau$ is $C^2$ and strictly increasing. [[lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization]] gives its $C^1$ inverse; its derivative $dt/d\tau=\gamma(t(\tau))$ is $C^1$, hence the inverse is $C^2$. Scaling to $\sigma=c\tau$ gives $dt/d\sigma=\gamma/c$. Thus $\Phi$ is $C^2$, its four derivative columns are $n,e_1,e_2,e_3$, and its determinant in the chart is $\gamma>0$. Its inverse is explicit from $t=x^0/c$, $\xi=x^1-q(t)$, $y=x^2,z=x^3$, so it is injective with open image and satisfies the precise $J\times B\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ family hypothesis of [[lem-sr-connecting-field-stretching]]. The $C^1$ field $n$ depends only on $t=x^0/c$. Using the first-order projected formula for $\theta$, and the fact that $s_\parallel$ is horizontal, Writing $\dot\beta=d\beta/dt$, the only nonzero coordinate derivatives are $\partial_0n_0=-\gamma^3\beta\dot\beta/c$ and $\partial_0n_1=\gamma^3\dot\beta/c$. Therefore $s_\parallel^a s_\parallel^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3\beta\dot\beta/c$, giving $\theta(s_\parallel,s_\parallel)=s_\parallel^a s_\parallel^b\partial_an_b=\gamma^3q\prime q\prime\prime/c^3$. This proves the formula with exactly $C^2$ data and agrees with [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]](d); it does not require a smooth-only supplier for the nonsmooth branch.
(c) Compute $h(e,e)=1+\gamma^2\beta^2=\gamma^2$ and $h(e)=e+\gamma\beta n=\gamma s_\parallel$. Since $\theta(n,\cdot)=0$, the difference of $e/\gamma$ and $s_\parallel$ is annihilated by $\theta$. Applying [[lem-sr-connecting-field-stretching]] to the four-dimensional family, then restricting to fixed transverse labels, gives $G=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma^2,1,1)$ and the length/rate identities. Independently $d\gamma/dt=\gamma^3q\prime q\prime\prime/c^2$ and $d/d\tau=\gamma d/dt$ give $d(\gamma L)/d\tau=\gamma^4Lq\prime q\prime\prime/c^2$. The derivative with respect to geometric proper length is instead $d/d\sigma=(\gamma/c)d/dt$. The length $\gamma L$ is exactly the integral of the pulled-back local rest metric over the fixed-label segment; the fixed-$\sigma$ segment need not lie in an endpoint observer's orthogonal hyperplane. The equality/constancy statements follow from $\gamma=(1-q\prime{}^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.
(d) Compare $\mathcal L(t)$ with $\mathcal L(0)=\gamma(0)L$. This gives the factor and the stretch/shrink cases without an initial-rest hypothesis. Specializing $q\prime(0)=0$ gives the original initially resting stretch conclusion. Material failure and constitutive stress require an additional model and are not deduced.
(e) Apply the exact smooth Rindler clause of [[thm-sr-fermi-walker-and-rigid-observer-examples]] and [[def-sr-proper-acceleration]]; its rigidity and unequal radial accelerations provide the stated contrast. (f) Retain all physical qualifications and the absence of empirical or material-dynamics conclusions.

items.physical_scope: A conditional kinematic thought experiment in flat classical special relativity about two prescribed rocket worldlines with equal chart-frame accelerations and a thread whose material points are modelled as following the translated congruence. It contains no dynamical or elastic model, no material failure criterion, no force law, no measurement and no empirical claim; breaking or tension of a real thread is explicitly not asserted, and no experimental data are used or invented. The preserved C2 worldline branch uses first-order C1 kinematics and an explicit C2 four-dimensional material family. Internal length gamma(t)L is compared with gamma(0)L; initial-rest stretch is a special case, and finite endpoint simultaneity distance is not identified without a separate construction.

items.title: Complex plane-wave fields: real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Fix $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, $\omega>0$ and $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Writing $\exp$ for the complex exponential, $\operatorname{Re}$ for the real part and $\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$ for the Euclidean inner product, define for each $t\in\mathbb R$ the real vector fields $$\mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf e\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr],\qquad \mathbf x\mapsto\operatorname{Re}\bigl[\mathbf b\exp(i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t))\bigr]$$ on $\mathbb R^3$, componentwise. Complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations; the complex object is not itself a physical field, and real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are explicit operations.
items.strategy: State the encoding convention and its regularity: the defining maps are smooth in $(\mathbf x,t)$ because the complex exponential is entire and $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t$ is linear. No electromagnetic interpretation is asserted; that is a later model choice.

references.title: Review of Phasor Notation (course notes, University of San Diego), Complex Vectors and Time Harmonic Representation; Amplitude, Time Average, Mean Square
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Moving parametrized surface patches and their flux
items.statement: Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a compact finite elementary Green region with its positive boundary orientation and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval. Let $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extend to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on the interior, and require the images to be embedded if an actual material sheet is intended. Define the velocity $v$ on a neighbourhood of the swept surface by $v(r(u,v,t),t):=\partial_tr(u,v,t)$, requiring it to be single-valued and of class $C^1$. For a $C^1$ field $B$ on a neighbourhood of the swept set, the flux through the patch at time $t$ is $$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(u,v,t),t),\,r_u(u,v,t)\times r_v(u,v,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv.$$
items.strategy: Elementary Green regions are compact Jordan-measurable parameter regions, so the flux is a Riemann integral, and the orientation is the patch orientation of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. Single-valuedness of the velocity is the hypothesis that makes the transport formula of the moving-flux lemma well posed. No physical assertion is made.

references.title: M. E. Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables, §3.2 and §4.4
J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)

items.title: Surface distributions and interfacial jumps
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$, and put $\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS$ for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, the surface integral being that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]. A continuous density $a$ on $S$ defines $a\delta_S(\psi)=\int_S a\psi\,dS$. Both functionals are continuous of finite order on test functions, because $\lvert a\rvert$ and $\psi$ are bounded on the compact interface and the surface measure is finite. A field that is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided continuous traces has locally integrable components; write $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ for the jump across $S$. The compact branch also localizes to a noncompact two-sided embedded $C^2$ interface that is closed in $\Omega$ (equivalently its inclusion is proper): for every compact test support $K$, $S\cap K$ is compact and admits finitely many regular graph patches. Its area integrals use the same compact Borel-face chart formula and finite ambient partition, not an assumed finite total area. If $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with both sides open and disjoint, this geometry already makes $S$ relatively closed. More generally, given a compatible chart-area measure on a possibly nonproper interface, a measurable density $a$ defines the weighted pairing directly whenever $\int_{S\cap K}|a|\,dS<\infty$ for every compact ambient $K$; the unweighted pairing requires this condition for $a=1$. No mere embeddedness or compactness of the test alone implies local mass finiteness. An ordinary continuous one-sided trace means an actual continuous extension of the field values to the closed side, locally near the interface; it is not an unspecified weak trace and does not imply integrability of classical derivatives. Such values are locally bounded, hence the fields are locally integrable in the compact/proper geometry. A one-sided $C^1$ extension additionally extends the first derivatives; this stronger condition is distinguished in [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]].
items.strategy: For a compact test support K and proper S, cover S intersect K by finitely many regular graph charts and split a neighbourhood of that compact set with [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]]. The compact Borel-face clause of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] applies in every chart; overlap and partition independence are exactly [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. In each chart the Gram density is bounded on the compact parameter support, so finitely many terms give finite area and finite mass for a continuous density. The bound |T_a(psi)|<=sup_K|psi| times the finite integral of |a| on S intersect K proves order-zero continuity by [[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]. The same estimate proves the conditional measurable-density branch when its local absolute mass is supplied, without asserting that an arbitrary nonproper embedding has it. The integral a delta_S there denotes the weighted pairing, not multiplication of an arbitrary distribution by a nonsmooth function. Ordinary continuous extensions of the values are bounded on each compact closed half-chart; off S use continuity, giving finite local bounds after a finite cover. Set [F]=F_+-F_- with the chosen minus-to-plus normal; extending values alone says nothing about first-derivative integrability.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Localization: vanishing integrals or fluxes force a continuous function to vanish
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and $g:U\to\mathbb R^m$ continuous. If $\int_Vg=0$ for every ball $V$ compactly contained in $U$, then $g=0$ on $U$. Moreover, in dimension $n=3$, if $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ is continuous and its flux through every disk of arbitrary center in every translated plane parallel to each of the three coordinate planes, with either fixed coordinate unit normal and every positive radius whose closed disk lies in $U$, is zero, then $F=0$ on $U$.
items.strategy: If $g(p)_i>0$, continuity gives a ball $V\Subset U$ on which $g_i\ge g_i(p)/2$; then $0<(g_i(p)/2)\lambda(V)\le\int_Vg_i$, contradicting the hypothesis. Apply to each component and to $-g_i$. For the disk statement fix p in U and a coordinate normal e_i. The affine plane through p perpendicular to e_i has a small closed disk centered at p contained in U. Its translated linear parameterization is regular and its area Jacobian is one, so the actual surface-flux definition identifies its flux with the two-dimensional Lebesgue integral of F_i on that disk. If F_i(p) has nonzero sign, continuity gives a smaller disk where its absolute value is bounded below by |F_i(p)|/2, and positive disk area gives a contradiction exactly as in the ball argument. Do this for i=1,2,3; disks only in the three origin planes would not suffice (F=(x_1 x_2 x_3,0,0) vanishes there). The general n-dimensional ball statement is unchanged and uses its own measurable-ball hypothesis, not a fixed physical test geometry. One special loop or box does not suffice. The disk parameter domain is the closed disk D_r centered at zero, with r>0: [[cor-disc-jordan-content-is-pi-r-squared]] supplies its compact Jordan measurability and positive content. The affine parameterization (u,v) to p+u e_j+v e_k is defined on all R2, injective, with constant nonzero cross product, so it satisfies the exact admissible regular-patch contract. The Riemann flux integral equals its two-dimensional Lebesgue value by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] applied to the continuous disk integrand and bounded zero extension to a rectangle. This justifies the comparison used above without importing physical fixed-test restrictions into the pure mathematical statement.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: Monopole-dipole expansion with an explicit remainder for compactly supported $L^1$ densities
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). Let $a>0$ and let $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ vanish $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere outside $\{y:\lvert y\rvert\le a\}$. Put $Q:=\int\rho$, $p:=\int y\,\rho(y)\,dy$ and $\lVert\rho\rVert_1:=\int\lvert\rho\rvert$. Then for every $x$ with $r:=\lvert x\rvert\ge2a>0$, $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y)}{\lvert x-y\rvert}\,dy=\frac Qr+\frac{p\cdot x}{r^3}+R(x),\qquad \lvert R(x)\rvert\le\frac{16\,a^2\lVert\rho\rVert_1}{r^3}.$$
items.strategy: Set $h(s)=\lvert x-sy\rvert^{-1}$; $h$ is $C^2$ on $[0,1]$ and the identity $h(1)-h(0)-h'(0)=\int_0^1(1-s)h''(s)\,ds$ follows from the fundamental theorem applied to $\frac{d}{ds}[(1-s)h'(s)+h(s)]=(1-s)h''(s)$. Because $\lvert x-sy\rvert\ge r-a\ge r/2$ for $r\ge2a$, one has $\lvert h''(s)\rvert\le4\lvert y\rvert^2/(r-a)^3\le32\lvert y\rvert^2/r^3$, and integrating against $\lvert\rho\rvert$ gives the bound with $C=16$, which is permissible but not sharp. Both leading terms follow directly by integrating h(0)=1/r and hprime(0)=(x dot y)/r³; no normalization-sensitive decay theorem is needed as a logical supplier. The parameter integral in $s\in[0,1]$ is a continuous Riemann integral, so [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] bounds it by $32|y|^2r^{-3}\int_0^1(1-s)ds=16|y|^2r^{-3}$. The subsequent integral against the $L^1$ source density is Lebesgue: its majorant $16a^2r^{-3}|\rho|$ is handled by [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]] and [[thm-integral-triangle-inequality]], not by the Darboux theorem. Both $Q$ and $p$ are finite by the same bounded-support estimate. No derivative bound on an unspecified remainder is inferred. Choose an a.e.-equal representative zero off the closed source ball. The integral equality and all moments are unchanged by [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]; every bound is thus valid for the declared a.e. support hypothesis.

references.title: J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7
S. Teitel, PHY 415 (University of Rochester), Unit 2-4: Electric Multipole Expansion

items.title: Differentiation under the integral sign over a compact measurable set and over a compact $C^1$ surface
items.statement: Let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be compact, measurable and of finite Lebesgue measure, let $a<b$, and let $f$ and $\partial_tf$ be continuous on a neighbourhood of $K\times[a,b]$. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$, with relative derivatives at the endpoints, and $\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,dx=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,dx$. The same conclusion holds, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], with surface measure on a fixed compact $C^1$ hypersurface in place of $K$ and Lebesgue measure. Nothing is asserted for moving parameter sets or for singularities crossing $K$.
items.strategy: For fixed $x$ the mean value theorem writes $[f(x,t+h)-f(x,t)]/h=\partial_tf(x,\tau)$ for some $\tau$ between $t$ and $t+h$; uniform continuity of $\partial_tf$ on the compact product bounds the integral of the difference by the sup-error times the finite measure. Iterate on finitely many charts, using the independence of the surface integral from the chart, for the surface clause.

references.title: J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Distributional continuity of a moving point charge
items.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval, $z:I\to\mathbb R^3$ a $C^1$ trajectory, and $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ open containing its graph. Assume the graph map $\gamma:I\to\Omega$, $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$, is proper: the inverse image of every compact subset of $\Omega$ is compact in $I$. For $q\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ define $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle=q\int_I\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle=q\int_I z'(t)\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$. These define distributions and $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Properness is automatic if $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, or if $I=\mathbb R$. Endpoint variant: if $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite, and both endpoint events belong to $\Omega$, the same integrals instead define distributions with $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)}$. A finite-history source is source-free only when the endpoint contribution vanishes on the chosen test domain; neither mere graph containment nor test compactness alone supplies this.
items.strategy: For a fixed compact test support $K\subset\Omega$, properness makes $\gamma^{-1}(K)$ compact in $I$. It lies in one closed interior interval $[u,v]\subset I$, on which $z'$ is bounded. Both pairings are bounded by constants depending on $K$ times $\sup_K|\psi|$, proving distribution continuity on each test-support space. The pullback of a test is $C^1$ and compactly supported in $I$. By the total chain rule, pairing the divergence gives $-q\int_I[\partial_t\psi(z(t),t)+z'(t)\cdot\nabla\psi(z(t),t)]dt=-q\int_I(d/dt)\psi(z(t),t)dt=0$ by interior FTC. For $I=\mathbb R$, compact ambient support bounds the time coordinate and its graph preimage is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R$; for $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$, compact ambient support has time projection compact inside $I$. This proves both automatic properness claims. In the endpoint variant, finite interval length and the finite absolute improper integral of $z'$ bound the pairings on every compact test support. Apply the chain rule and FTC on $[a+\epsilon,b-\epsilon]$; the derivative pullback is absolutely integrable, and continuity at endpoints gives the limiting identity $q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)$. This proves the two endpoint deltas. In particular $I=(0,1),z=0,\Omega=\mathbb R^4$ gives $q\delta_{(0,0)}-q\delta_{(0,1)}$, refuting the old unconditional claim. The endpoint integration limit is explicitly this truncation argument, not an invented source reading. Maxwell existence and point self-force are not asserted. Here the two-ended improper integral means the sum of the limits of integrals on [a+epsilon,r] and [r,b−epsilon] for any fixed interior r. Monotonicity and completeness prove convergence of every nonnegative integrand bounded by a constant times 1+|z′|; signed limits then follow from the positive and negative parts. Thus the endpoint variant uses only the explicitly supplied improper convention and truncated ordinary FTC.

references.title: S. Dyatlov, Lecture notes for 18.155 (MIT, 2026), Chapter 2 and Chapter 3
J. K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (UC Davis, 2014), §1.10, §1.12, §2.7

items.title: Quadratic stress identity and the local angular-balance identity
items.statement: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$. Put $Q_{ij}:=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2$, where $\delta_{ij}=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise, and $(\operatorname{div}Q)_i:=\sum_j\partial_jQ_{ij}$. Then $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$. Moreover, writing $\epsilon_{ijk}$ for the Levi-Civita symbol ($+1$ on even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ on odd ones, $0$ otherwise), every $C^1$ symmetric tensor satisfies $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0$, and if $\partial_tg+\operatorname{div}\Pi=-f$ with $\Pi$ symmetric, $\operatorname{div}\Pi$ taken as $(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_i=\sum_\ell\partial_\ell\Pi_{i\ell}$ and $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}:=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$, then $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$.
items.strategy: Expand $\sum_j\partial_j(F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\lvert F\rvert^2)=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_jF_j\partial_jF_i-\sum_jF_j\partial_iF_j$ by the product rule; the last difference is $-(F\times\operatorname{curl}F)_i$. For the second part, expand $\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}$ and cancel the two equal terms using symmetry; the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes. No symmetry of $Q$ beyond the displayed form is needed.

references.title: J. Feldman, A. Rechnitzer, E. Yeager, CLP-4 Vector Calculus (UBC), §4.1 (Theorems 4.1.4-4.1.16)

items.title: Distributional divergence and curl across a stationary interface
items.statement: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $S$ be a two-sided compact embedded $C^2$ interface with unit normal $n$ from minus to plus. The same local conclusions hold for an interface closed in $\Omega$, with tests supported away from any edge. Let $F$ be $C^1$ on the open sides and have ordinary continuous extensions of its values to each closed side near $S$, as in [[def-em-surface-distribution]]. For each component there is a canonical bulk distribution $\mathcal B_{ij}$, equal to the classical $\partial_iF_j$ away from $S$, such that $$\partial_iT_{F_j}=\mathcal B_{ij}+n_i[F_j]\delta_S.$$ Thus $\operatorname{div}T_F=\sum_i\mathcal B_{ii}+n\cdot[F]\delta_S$ and $(\operatorname{curl}T_F)_k=\sum_{i,j}\epsilon_{kij}\mathcal B_{ij}+(n\times[F])_k\delta_S$. The bulk distribution is the graph-truncated classical-derivative limit specified below; it need not be a regular locally integrable function. If the piecewise classical first derivatives are locally absolutely integrable across $S$, then $\mathcal B_{ij}=T_{\{\partial_iF_j\}_{\rm piecewise}}$, giving the original regular-bulk divergence and curl identities. In particular this regular specialization applies when the field and its first derivatives have one-sided $C^1$ extensions to the closed sides. Continuous trace values alone are not that stronger hypothesis. No moving-interface formula is asserted.
items.strategy: Fix a compact test supported away from edges. Properness makes its interface intersection compact; use the finite ambient partition to reduce to finitely many graph cylinders, plus interior patches. For a graph z=g(y), trim the sides at z=g(y)-epsilon and z=g(y)+epsilon, keeping the localized test zero near the cylinder's other faces. On each trimmed finite piecewise C1 domain the field is C1 on its compact closure, so [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]] applies to psi F_j e_i. It gives the classical derivative integral as minus the F_j derivative-of-test integral minus its outward boundary integral. The two graph faces have the same Gram density and normals tending to n and -n; ordinary continuous value extensions give uniform convergence on the compact parameter support. The omitted bulk layer contributes at most its shrinking volume times a uniform bound on F_j and the derivative of psi. Consequently the sum of the trimmed derivative integrals converges to -integral F_j partial_i psi - integral_S n_i[F_j]psi. Define B_ij by this limit. It equals partial_i T_Fj minus n_i[F_j]delta_S, so is a distribution of order at most one; this intrinsic expression proves independence of graph covers and partitions. It agrees with the classical derivative on tests away from S. If the piecewise derivative is L1loc, [[thm-dominated-convergence]] with its absolute value on the compact test support identifies the truncated limit with its ordinary integral. A C1 extension of field and derivatives gives bounded derivatives on each compact closed half-chart and hence this L1 condition. Taking the trace or antisymmetric sum proves divergence and curl with exactly the stated normal sign. For a continuous-value trace without derivative integrability, retain the canonical distributional bulk: for example z sin(z^-2) above z=0, extended by zero below, has continuous trace zero but its classical normal derivative is not locally absolutely integrable. No invalid regular-bulk conclusion is imposed on that branch.

items.title: Joint regularity of radial vector and scalar potentials on star-shaped domains
items.statement: Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval I: a map on $U\times I$ is jointly $C^k$ when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$; jointly $C^\infty$ means the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open I these are exactly the usual open-domain classes of def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms. At included endpoints of a nondegenerate time interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton I the restriction convention still asserts extension existence and the stated spatial identities, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. This convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded I. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be of class $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$. Then the radial witness $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is $C^k$ jointly with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ for every $t$, then the radial scalar witness $\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-a\rangle\,ds$ is $C^k$ jointly on $U\times I$ and $\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t$. For $C^\infty$ data both potentials are $C^\infty$ jointly. No global potential on an arbitrary open set is claimed.
items.strategy:
The interval regularity convention is supplied explicitly in the statement, rather than treating the imported open-domain definition as already covering non-open products. To prove regularity in that same extension sense, choose an open-neighbourhood Ck extension of the data (intersect the extensions' neighbourhoods if both B and C are used). Let P be the set of (x,t) for which every (a+s(x-a),t), 0<=s<=1, lies in that open extension domain. It contains UxI by star-shapedness. It is open: at any one point of P its compact radial segment has a finite cover by balls contained in the extension domain; equivalently its distance from the closed complement is positive, and continuity of the radial map uniformly in s keeps all nearby (x,t) segments inside those balls. The identical radial integral of the extension data is therefore defined on P and is Ck there by the compact parameter proof below; its restriction is the stated potential. For smooth input use its one smooth extension and the same argument through every finite order. Curl-freeness/divergence-freeness is only needed on the original slices to establish the field identities there, not on the enlarged neighbourhood. Set w=x-a and z_s=a+sw. The spatial star-shaped hypothesis puts z_s in U for 0<=s<=1. For any compact spatial box Q contained in U and compact parameter subinterval J contained in I, the radial image of [0,1]xQ is compact inside U. Each component of the vector and scalar radial integrands is a finite sum of products of the polynomial factors s,w and the Ck components of B(z_s,t) or C(z_s,t). Chain and product rules give every mixed spatial/time word derivative through total order k as a continuous function of (s,x,t) on the corresponding compact product. Apply thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign-on-a-compact-rectangle in each parameter coordinate, with others fixed, and induct on derivative order. Uniform continuity on the compact product and lem-uniform-integral-error-bound show that each resulting derivative integral is jointly continuous. Included endpoints of nondegenerate time intervals use the relative endpoint derivatives of the compact-rectangle supplier. For empty or singleton I, construct the potentials using a chosen ambient extension on its open radial-admissibility set and restrict; this proves the same extension existence and spatial identities, without claiming uniquely determined time jets on the degenerate restriction. Thus both explicit integrals are jointly Ck, without assuming k+1 derivatives, and applying this for every k gives the smooth assertion. No surface-measure or Lebesgue integration/Choice branch of lem-em-parameter-integrals is needed: these are ordinary one-dimensional integrals in s on [0,1].

At each fixed t, the positive vector integral is exactly the witness of thm-a-divergence-free-c1-field-on-a-star-shaped-open-set-has-a-vector-potential, so curl A=B. For the scalar branch put Psi_C(x,t)=integral_0^1 <C(z_s,t),w> ds, and take phi_C=-Psi_C. The published Poincare theorem gives grad Psi_C=C; its convention is positive gradient, so it cannot itself justify grad of the positive integral being -C. Explicitly, curl C=0 means partial_j C_i=partial_i C_j in three dimensions. Differentiation gives partial_j Psi_C=integral_0^1 [C_j(z_s,t)+s sum_i w_i partial_j C_i(z_s,t)] ds. Replace partial_j C_i by partial_i C_j; the integrand becomes d/ds[s C_j(z_s,t)]. thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative gives C_j(x,t)-0*C_j(a,t)=C_j(x,t), hence partial_j phi_C=-C_j. Therefore grad phi_C=-C with the stated finite-k and smooth joint regularity. In particular for C=e1, phi_C=-(x1-a1), so grad phi_C=-e1; the old positive integral gave +e1 and was a concrete contradiction. Neither a general non-star-shaped global existence claim nor a new physical assumption is introduced. On a ball the same construction is local even when the surrounding open set has holes; scalar circulation and vector-flux obstructions remain distinct.

items.title: Transport of flux through a moving patch
items.statement: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]], let $B$ be a $C^1$ field on a neighbourhood of the swept surface with $\operatorname{div}B=0$. Then $\Phi$ is differentiable on $I$ and $$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r,$$ the boundary integral using the induced orientation. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term $\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$ appears.
items.strategy: Differentiate the parametrized flux with the parameter lemma; the area derivative contributes $\partial_uv\times r_v+r_u\times\partial_vv$, and collecting terms gives $[\partial_tB+(v\cdot\nabla)B+B\operatorname{div}v-(B\cdot\nabla)v]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$. The published cross-product identity turns this into $[\partial_tB+v\operatorname{div}B-\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)]\cdot(r_u\times r_v)$, and patch Stokes converts the curl term into the boundary circulation. The $C^2$ hypothesis lets mixed derivatives commute. Lorentz-force interpretation is a separate physical premise.

references.title: I. Galili, D. Kaplan, Y. Lehavi, Teaching Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction in an introductory physics course, Am. J. Phys. 74, 337 (2006), Appendix

items.title: Period averages of products of real parts of complex exponentials
items.statement: Let $\omega>0$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, and let $a,d\in\mathbb C$ (or $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, componentwise). Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})\operatorname{Re}(de^{-i\omega t})\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(a\overline d),$$ and the dot-product and cross-product versions hold componentwise. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation.
items.strategy: Write $\operatorname{Re}(z)=(z+\overline z)/2$; the product is one constant term $\frac14(a\overline d+\overline ad)$ plus oscillatory terms $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$, which integrate to zero over a full period by the fundamental theorem applied to $e^{\pm2i\omega t}/(\pm2i\omega)$.

J. Lebl, Basic Analysis II, §9.1 (Leibniz integral rule), Theorem 9.1.1

items.title: The two-equation interface system at normal incidence
items.statement: Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for $j=1,2$, and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$ Then $E_r/E_i=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$, $E_t/E_i=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, and $R:=\lvert E_r/E_i\rvert^2$, $T:=(Z_1/Z_2)\lvert E_t/E_i\rvert^2$ satisfy $R+T=1$. The two equations are assumed, not derived; oblique incidence, complex impedance and anisotropy require further systems and branch conventions.
items.strategy: Solve the $2\times2$ system by substitution; its determinant is $Z_1+Z_2>0$. For $R+T=1$, substitute the ratios and use $(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2=(Z_1+Z_2)^2$. No electromagnetic validity is asserted.

references.title: R. Fitzpatrick, Electromagnetism lecture notes (UT Austin), Reflection at a dielectric boundary, Eqs. (1210)-(1232)

items.title: Linear and affine Lorentz maps, and the Lorentz group
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be a 4-dimensional Lorentz vector space (def-lorentz-form-and-inertia) with a chosen time orientation C^+ (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets), and let (A,V,eta,C^+) be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model). (a) A linear Lorentz map is a linear map L: V -> V such that eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V. The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted O(V,eta). (b) If (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) is an ordered eta-orthonormal basis of V (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis), eta_0 := diag(-1,1,1,1) is the matrix of eta in it, and M is the matrix of L in that basis (def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map), then L is a linear Lorentz map if and only if M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; every linear Lorentz map is a linear isomorphism, and the condition does not depend on the eta-orthonormal basis used. (c) A linear Lorentz map L is proper if det L = +1 and orthochronous if L(C^+) = C^+; the set of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps is denoted SO^+(V,eta). O(V,eta) is called the (full) Lorentz group of (V,eta) and SO^+(V,eta) the proper orthochronous Lorentz group; that these are groups under composition is proved in lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (d) An affine Lorentz map is a map F: A -> A for which there exist p_0 in A and a linear Lorentz map L with F(p_0 + v) = F(p_0) + L v for all v in V; equivalently F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) for all p in A, and L is then unique. F is called proper (resp. orthochronous) when L is. If x is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x(F(p)) = M x(p) + b for all p, where M is the matrix of L in the frame's ordered basis and b := x(F(o)) - M x(o) in R^4. (e) In this framework, unless stated otherwise, 'Lorentz transformation' means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map; improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly (the B-page counterexample names the parity and time-reversal matrices).
items.strategy: A definition item: it fixes the language of the page and makes no proof claim beyond what lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure establishes (the matrix criterion, invertibility and the group structure, which is listed as justified_by). The well-definedness obligations are: (i) the set O(V,eta) is defined by a property of linear maps on the fixed vector space V, so it is a set; (ii) the matrix criterion in (b) must be stated in an ordered eta-orthonormal basis, whose existence is the cited lemma, and its independence of that choice is part of the proved content; (iii) 'L(C^+) = C^+' is a condition on a map of sets, not a notation for an unproved continuity statement; (iv) the affine definition (d) must distinguish an active map F on the point set A from the coordinate expression in a chart, and must not conflate an affine map with a general chart change; the coordinate expression requires the identification of vectors with coordinate columns and the cited matrix conventions. The exposition may state that the linear part of an affine Lorentz map is recovered as L v = F(p+v) - F(p), independently of p.

items.title: The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta
items.statement: Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), and let x = (x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3) be its coordinates, so that a vector is written x = x^0 e_0 + x^1 e_1 + x^2 e_2 + x^3 e_3 and the spatial part is the coordinate column x_vec = (x^1,x^2,x^3) of R^3 with its standard Euclidean structure (def-euclidean-inner-product). For beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1, where |beta| is the Euclidean norm, set gamma(beta) := (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) >= 1, with equality exactly for beta=0 and strict inequality for beta!=0 (def-rational-power, lem-rational-power-laws). The passive Lorentz boost with parameter beta is the linear map B(beta): V -> V defined by its action on coordinates: for beta not equal to 0, x'^0 = gamma (x^0 - beta . x),  x' = x + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2)(beta . x) beta - gamma beta x^0, and for beta = 0, B(0) := identity, where x' denotes the coordinates of B(beta) applied to the vector with coordinates x, and beta . x is the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis (e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) the matrix of B(beta) is B^0_0 = gamma, B^0_i = B^i_0 = -gamma beta_i for i = 1,2,3, and B^i_j = delta^i_j + ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) beta_i beta_j for i,j = 1,2,3 (with the last expression replaced by delta^i_j for beta = 0; the coefficient (gamma−1)/|beta|^2 tends to 1/2 as beta tends to0 through nonzero vectors, so the correction is (1/2) beta_i beta_j+o(|beta|^2) and the full spatial block tends to delta^i_j). In the 1+1 case beta = beta e_1 this reads x'^0 = gamma(x^0 - beta x^1), x'^1 = gamma(x^1 - beta x^0). The vector beta is called the boost parameter; it is dimensionless and mathematically independent of any unit convention.
items.strategy: A definition item, well-defined because the displayed formulas assign to every coordinate pair (x^0,x_vec) a pair (x'^0,x'_vec), and by thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis (applied through def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map) there is a unique linear map with that matrix, namely x |-> E o M o E^{-1}. The beta = 0 case is declared separately because the matrix expression ((gamma - 1)/|beta|^2) is undefined there; the definition must not silently divide by zero, and the stated limit follows from the explicit rationalization below. This item asserts no Lorentz property: that B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and that B(-beta) is its inverse is the content of lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse, and the composition law is the content of lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition; the physical reading of c beta as a relative velocity is stated only on the physics items of this page, not here. For the gamma boundary, gamma is positive and gamma^2=1/(1−|beta|^2)>=1, with equality exactly when |beta|=0, so gamma>=1 with precisely the asserted equality case. For beta!=0 the identity gamma^2−1=|beta|^2 gamma^2 yields (gamma−1)/|beta|^2=gamma^2/(gamma+1). Continuity of the positive power in [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]] makes gamma tend to1 as beta tends to0, hence that coefficient tends to1/2. Multiplication by beta_i beta_j proves the leading correction and full spatial-block limit: |beta_i beta_j|<=|beta|^2, so [gamma^2/(gamma+1)−1/2]beta_i beta_j=o(|beta|^2). Thus B(beta) tends to the separately declared identity without a hidden division by zero. No physical velocity interpretation is added. Real and rational powers are identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. The Euclidean norm convention gives $|\beta_i|^2\le\sum_k\beta_k^2=|\beta|^2$, hence $|\beta_i|\le|\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\beta|^2$. In the norm meaning of $\beta\to0$, $|\beta|\to0$. For $|\beta|^2\le3/4$ one has $1\le\gamma\le2$, so $|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\beta|\to0$; also $\gamma-1=|\beta|^2\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)\to0$. Together with the already proved spatial-block limit these are every matrix entry of $B(\beta)\to I$.

items.title: Spatial rotations of an inertial frame
items.statement: Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model and let S := span(e_1,e_2,e_3) be its spatial three-space with delta the restriction of eta to S (def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame); delta is a positive-definite symmetric bilinear form, (e_1,e_2,e_3) is delta-orthonormal, and S = {w in V : eta(e_0,w) = 0}. A spatial rotation of the frame is a linear map R: V -> V such that R(e_0) = e_0, R(S) is contained in S (so that the restriction R|_S is an endomorphism of S; the determinant condition below forces R(S) = S) and delta(Rw,Rz) = delta(w,z) for all w,z in S, and whose restriction R|_S has determinant +1 computed in the ordered basis (e_1,e_2,e_3). Via the delta-orthonormal basis (e_1,e_2,e_3), these maps are exactly the linear maps whose matrix is a 3x3 matrix A with A^T A = I_3 and det A = +1; such matrices form the group SO(3), and the spatial rotations of the frame form a subgroup of the general linear group of V isomorphic to SO(3) (def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator, cor-orthogonal-and-unitary-operators-form-groups-and-have-unit-determinant-modulus). The extension by R(e_0) = e_0 of a spatial rotation is also written R.
items.strategy: A definition item with its well-definedness resting on the published positive-definite orthogonal-operator material already supplied by def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame (positivity of delta on S and the orthonormal basis) and by the cited corollary (orthogonal operators with determinant modulus one form a group; the determinant-one subset is a subgroup). The definition must separate three objects: the geometric spatial three-space S of a named frame, the restriction R|_S which is the actual rotation, and the extension by the identity on the time direction. The determinant is taken with respect to the orientation of S induced by the ordered basis (e_1,e_2,e_3), which the frame definition fixes; a change of frame changes which maps are called spatial rotations. No claim is made here that spatial rotations are Lorentz maps (that is proved in lem-boost-rotation-factorization).

items.title: Lorentz maps are isomorphisms of determinant +-1 that preserve causal character and permute the cones; the Lorentz sets are groups
items.statement: Let L: V -> V be a linear map with eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V (def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group). Then: (i) L is a linear isomorphism of V; for every ordered eta-orthonormal basis the matrix M of L satisfies M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 with eta_0 = diag(-1,1,1,1), and conversely every invertible matrix M with M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that basis. (ii) det L = +-1. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map; the sets SO(V,eta) := {L : det L = 1}, O^up(V,eta) := {L : L(C^+) = C^+} and SO^+(V,eta) = SO(V,eta) intersect O^up(V,eta) are subgroups of O(V,eta), which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group GL(V). (iii) eta(Lv,Lv) = eta(v,v) for all v in V; hence L preserves the causal character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the set of null vectors onto itself. If L is proper, then the oriented volume form is preserved: epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) for all v_0,...,v_3 in V (def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form); if det L = -1 the two sides differ by the sign -1. (iv) L(C^+) is one of the two components C^+, C^- of the timelike set, so exactly one of L(C^+) = C^+ and L(C^+) = C^- holds; L is orthochronous in the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and L(C^+) = C^+ holds if and only if L(C^+) is contained in C^+. (v) The affine Lorentz maps (def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group(d)) form a group under composition: the composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps, and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of A.
items.strategy: Proof plan. (i) If Lv = 0 then eta(v,w) = eta(Lv,Lw) = 0 for every w, so v = 0 by nondegeneracy of eta; hence L is injective and, V being finite-dimensional, an isomorphism. Writing vectors in an eta-orthonormal basis, the identity eta(Lv,Lw) = eta(v,w) becomes v^T M^T eta_0 M w = v^T eta_0 w for all coordinate columns v,w, which by nondegeneracy of the pairing is equivalent to M^T eta_0 M = eta_0; the converse direction defines L by v |-> E(M(E^{-1}(v))) and computes the same identity. (ii) Taking determinants in M^T eta_0 M = eta_0 and using det eta_0 = -1, det(M^T) = det M and thm-determinant-multiplicative gives (det M)^2 = 1, so det L = +-1. Closure of O(V,eta) under composition: eta(LMv,LMw) = eta(Mv,Mw) = eta(v,w). Identity and inverses: eta(L^{-1}v,L^{-1}w) = eta(LL^{-1}v,LL^{-1}w) = eta(v,w), using L(L^{-1}v) = v. The determinant conditions are preserved because det is multiplicative (thm-determinant-multiplicative, cor-determinant-of-an-inverse), and orthochrony is preserved because LM(C^+) = L(C^+) = C^+ and L^{-1}(C^+) = C^+ when L(C^+) = C^+. Being a subgroup of GL(V) uses that GL(V) is a group (cor-general-linear-group-is-a-group) and def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map. (iii) The first identity is the defining property evaluated on (v,v). Since the sign of eta(v,v) is unchanged, the causal class of every nonzero v is unchanged, and null vectors are exactly those nonzero v with eta(v,v) = 0. For the volume form: in the frame's basis write the columns v_j, so epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) = det([v_j]) by def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form; then epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = det(M [v_j]) = det(M) det([v_j]) by multiplicativity, which equals epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) when det M = 1. (iv) L(C^+) is the continuous image of the connected set C^+ (lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components), hence connected, and it is contained in the timelike set because eta(Lv,Lv) = eta(v,v) < 0; a connected subset of the timelike set lies in one of its two components (def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets, lem-timelike-cone-has-two-convex-components). Since L is a bijection with L^{-1} also Lorentz, L maps the timelike set onto itself, so L(C^+) and L(C^-) are two nonempty components and hence are C^+ and C^- in some order; in particular L(C^+) = C^+ iff L(C^+) is contained in C^+. (v) If F(p) = F(p_0) + L(p - p_0) and G(p) = G(q_0) + M(p - q_0), then (G o F)(p) = G(F(p_0)) + ML(p - p_0) with ML Lorentz by closure; the inverse of F is p |-> p_0 + L^{-1}(p - F(p_0)), affine Lorentz with linear part L^{-1}, and the identity is affine Lorentz with L = id. There is no unproved step: every algebraic statement is a direct substitution, and the only topological input is the two-component structure of the timelike set, supplied by the cited predecessor lemma.

items.title: The passive boost is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse B(-beta)
items.statement: Let B(beta) be the passive boost of def-lorentz-boost in an inertial frame (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3). For every beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1 the following hold. (i) B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map: eta(B(beta)v,B(beta)w) = eta(v,w) for all v,w in V, det B(beta) = +1, and B(beta)(C^+) = C^+. (ii) B(0) is the identity, and for every beta the image of the frame vector e_0 is B(beta)e_0 = gamma(e_0 - beta_1 e_1 - beta_2 e_2 - beta_3 e_3), so the map beta |-> B(beta) is injective and B(beta) fixes the origin; moreover for every vector y with coordinates (0,y_vec) and beta . y = 0 one has B(beta)y = y. (iii) B(-beta)B(beta) = B(beta)B(-beta) = identity; in particular B(beta) is invertible with B(beta)^{-1} = B(-beta), and B(beta) and B(-beta) are inverse bijections of V. (iv) If u is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates (u^0,u_vec), so that eta(u,u) = -1 and u^0 > 0, and |u_vec| < u^0, then the boost with parameter beta := u_vec/u^0 satisfies B(beta)u = e_0. (v) If a vector x has x^0 > |x_vec|, then the first coordinate of B(beta)x is gamma(x^0 - beta . x) > 0; if x^0 < -|x_vec| then the first coordinate of B(beta)x is negative. In particular B(beta) maps the future open cone {x^0 > |x_vec|} into itself.
items.strategy: Proof plan, for beta not equal to 0 (the case beta = 0 is the identity, for which (i)-(v) are immediate). Put b := |beta| and e := beta/b, so (e_0,e) is an eta-orthonormal pair spanning a timelike 2-plane P, and V = P direct-sum P^perp with P^perp := {y : y^0 = 0 and beta . y = 0}, on which eta is positive definite. By construction B(beta) fixes P^perp pointwise (this is (ii)'s last clause) and on P its matrix in the basis (e_0,e) is [[gamma,-gamma b],[-gamma b,gamma]]. (i) For v = (v^0, v_parallel e + v_perp) and w likewise, eta(Bv,Bw) expands into the P-block computed by matrix multiplication, using gamma^2(1 - b^2) = 1 and gamma^2 b^2 + 1 = gamma^2, plus the P^perp-block and the vanishing of the cross terms (P perpendicular to P^perp); this gives eta(Bv,Bw) = eta(v,w). The determinant is the 2x2 determinant gamma^2(1 - b^2) = 1 times the identity on P^perp, hence +1. For the future cone: beta . x <= b|x_vec| < b x^0 whenever x^0 > |x_vec| >= 0, so x^0 - beta . x > x^0(1 - b) > 0; then B(beta)(C^+) is contained in C^+ (it is contained in the future open cone and connected), and since B(beta) is a Lorentz map with inverse B(-beta) (proved next) that also maps C^+ into C^+, one gets B(beta)(C^+) = C^+. The inequality beta . x <= b|x_vec| uses the Cauchy-Schwarz/triangle inequality for the Euclidean form, and (i) then follows from lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure. (ii) Evaluating the defining formulas at the coordinates of e_0 gives (gamma, -gamma beta_1, -gamma beta_2, -gamma beta_3); injectivity follows because the spatial coordinates of B(beta)e_0 determine beta and the time coordinate determines gamma. (iii) On P the two matrices multiply to gamma^2(1 - b^2) times the identity, using gamma^2(1 - b^2) = 1; on P^perp both are the identity. Hence B(-beta)B(beta) = B(beta)B(-beta) = identity. (iv) Since u is future timelike unit, |u_vec|^2 = (u^0)^2 - 1 < (u^0)^2, so |beta| = |u_vec|/u^0 < 1 and B(beta) is defined; substituting x = u into the formulas in the (e_0,e)-frame with e = beta/|beta| gives spatial part zero and first coordinate gamma(u^0 - beta . u) = gamma(u^0 - |u_vec|^2/u^0) = gamma((u^0)^2 - |u_vec|^2)/u^0 = gamma/u^0 = 1, using gamma = (1 - |beta|^2)^(-1/2) and the unit condition. (v) is the inequality computed in (i). Every step is a finite computation from the definition; the cited predecessor lemma supplies the conclusion that B(beta) is Lorentz, proper and orthochronous.

items.title: Collinear boost composition and the relativistic velocity-addition law
items.statement: Let B(beta_1 e) and B(beta_2 e) be passive boosts in a common spatial direction e, where e is a unit vector of the frame's spatial three-space and beta_1, beta_2 in (-1,1) are real parameters (def-lorentz-boost, def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame). Then B(beta_1 e) B(beta_2 e) = B(beta e) with beta := (beta_1 + beta_2)/(1 + beta_1 beta_2), and |beta| < 1; in particular the two collinear boosts commute, B(beta_1 e)B(beta_2 e) = B(beta_2 e)B(beta_1 e), and B(beta_1 e) B(-beta_2 e) = B(((beta_1 - beta_2)/(1 - beta_1 beta_2)) e). The parameter is accordingly additive under composition (velocity addition in units of the conversion constant: if beta_i are the dimensionless parameters, the composed parameter is the displayed beta and not beta_1 + beta_2), and no composition of two boosts in a common direction ever leaves the open interval (-1,1).
items.strategy: Compute the product of the two matrices on the common (e_0,e)-plane: both boosts act as the identity on the common perpendicular P^perp; when either parameter is0 that boost is the identity on all V, and the following plane calculation also covers this case, so the product is again the identity on P^perp and the 2x2 matrix product [[gamma_1,-gamma_1 beta_1],[-gamma_1 beta_1,gamma_1]] [[gamma_2,-gamma_2 beta_2],[-gamma_2 beta_2,gamma_2]] equals gamma_1 gamma_2 (1 + beta_1 beta_2) [[1, -(beta_1+beta_2)/(1+beta_1 beta_2)], [-(beta_1+beta_2)/(1+beta_1 beta_2), 1]], which is the boost matrix with parameter beta given above and gamma = gamma_1 gamma_2 (1 + beta_1 beta_2). The algebra proving the display uses gamma_i^2 (1 - beta_i^2) = 1 and the rational power laws. To see |beta| < 1: the denominator 1 + beta_1 beta_2 > 0 because |beta_1 beta_2| < 1, and |beta_1 + beta_2| < 1 + beta_1 beta_2 is equivalent to (beta_1 + beta_2)^2 < (1 + beta_1 beta_2)^2, i.e. to (1 - beta_1^2)(1 - beta_2^2) > 0, which holds since |beta_i| < 1. The minus case is the same multiplication with beta_2 replaced by -beta_2 and 1 - beta_1 beta_2 > 0. Since the identity on P^perp and the matrices on P together define the whole map, the computation is complete; no continuity or limiting argument is used.

items.title: Rapidity parametrization of collinear boosts
items.statement: For beta in (-1,1) define r(beta) := (1/2) log((1 + beta)/(1 - beta)), where log is the natural logarithm (def-natural-logarithm); the argument is positive because 1 + beta > 0 and 1 - beta > 0. Then r is a strictly increasing bijection of (-1,1) onto R. Writing sinh(r) := (e^r - e^(-r))/2, cosh(r) := (e^r + e^(-r))/2 and tanh(r) := sinh(r)/cosh(r) (def-real-exponential-function-and-e), one has cosh^2(r) - sinh^2(r) = 1, beta = tanh(r(beta)), (1 - tanh(r)^2)^(-1/2) = cosh(r), and sinh(r) = tanh(r) cosh(r) = beta gamma(beta) at beta = tanh(r). Consequently, for every unit spatial vector e the passive boost acts, in the ordered pair of directions (e_0,e), as the 2x2 matrix [[cosh r, -sinh r],[-sinh r, cosh r]] and as the identity on the perpendicular complement of the plane span(e_0,e). Finally, collinear rapidities add: for all r,s in R, B(tanh(r) e) B(tanh(s) e) = B(tanh(r + s) e), consistent with lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition.
items.strategy: Proof plan. (a) r is strictly increasing on (-1,1): the map beta |-> (1 + beta)/(1 - beta) has positive derivative 2/(1 - beta)^2 and log is strictly increasing (def-natural-logarithm is the inverse of the strictly increasing exp, thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing); the limits are -infinity and +infinity, so r is onto R by the intermediate value property. (b) beta = tanh(r(beta)): let q := e^(2r) = (1 + beta)/(1 - beta), then tanh(r) = (q - 1)/(q + 1) = beta by elementary algebra of the exponential. (c) Setting beta = tanh(r), the identity 1 - tanh^2 r = 1/cosh^2 r follows from cosh^2 r - sinh^2 r = 1 (itself an expansion using the exponential addition formula thm-exponential-addition-formula); since cosh r > 0, (1 - tanh^2 r)^(-1/2) = cosh r, and gamma(tanh r) = cosh r, sinh r = tanh r cosh r. (d) The matrix display is the definition of B(beta) evaluated at beta = tanh r, using gamma = cosh r and gamma beta = sinh r: [[gamma,-gamma beta],[-gamma beta,gamma]] = [[cosh r,-sinh r],[-sinh r,cosh r]]. (e) Finally the composition statement follows either from the matrix product with the addition formulas for sinh and cosh or from the composition lemma together with the addition law of the exponential; the two routes agree. The exponential presentation exp(r N_e) of the same matrix is supplied separately in lem-lorentz-exponential-map-and-rapidity, which depends on this item, so that this item does not presuppose the exponential series for matrices.

items.title: Unique boost-rotation factorization of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps
items.statement: Let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame, let S := span(e_1,e_2,e_3) be its spatial three-space and let L be a proper orthochronous Lorentz map (def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group). Write u := L e_0, with coordinates (u^0,u_vec) in the frame, and note eta(u,u) = -1 and u^0 > 0. Then (i) |u_vec| < u^0 and the parameter beta := u_vec/u^0 satisfies |beta| < 1; (ii) the linear map Rhat := B(beta) L satisfies Rhat(e_0) = e_0 and Rhat(S) = S, and its restriction to S is a spatial rotation of the frame in the sense of def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame; hence Rhat = diag(1,R) for the unique spatial rotation R with Rhat|_S = R, and L = B(-beta) Rhat, a product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation; (iii) conversely, for every beta with |beta| < 1 and every spatial rotation R of the frame, the extension Rhat = diag(1,R) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and the product B(-beta) Rhat is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map; (iv) the factorization L = B(-beta) Rhat of (ii) is unique: if B(-beta_1) Rhat_1 = B(-beta_2) Rhat_2 with |beta_i| < 1 and spatial rotations Rhat_i, then beta_1 = beta_2 and R_1 = R_2; (v) L is a passive boost, i.e. L = B(beta') for some |beta'| < 1, if and only if the rotation R in (ii) is the identity, and then beta' = -beta with beta the parameter of (i).
items.strategy: Proof plan. (i) From eta(u,u) = -1 one has |u_vec|^2 = (u^0)^2 - 1, and u^0 > 0 because L is orthochronous, so |u_vec| < u^0. (ii) By lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse(iv), B(beta)u = e_0 with beta := u_vec/u^0; since L e_0 = u this gives Rhat e_0 = B(beta) L e_0 = e_0. Rhat is a composition of Lorentz maps, hence Lorentz (lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure), and it preserves S = e_0^perp because for w in S, eta(e_0,Rhat w) = eta(Rhat e_0, Rhat w) = eta(e_0,w) = 0. Hence Rhat maps S into S and, being invertible, onto S; on S it preserves delta because delta is the restriction of eta. For the determinant: Rhat has block matrix diag(1, Rhat|_S) in the frame; det Rhat = det(Rhat|_S) and det Rhat = det B(beta) det L = 1, so det(Rhat|_S) = 1, and Rhat|_S is a spatial rotation. The representation Rhat = diag(1,R) and the equation L = B(beta)^{-1}Rhat = B(-beta)Rhat are then immediate. (iii) A spatial rotation Rhat fixes e_0 and preserves delta on S; expanding eta(Rhat v, Rhat w) in components (v^0,w^0 in the time direction and delta on S) gives eta(Rhat v,Rhat w) = eta(v,w), so Rhat is a Lorentz map; det Rhat = det R = 1, so it is proper, and it is orthochronous because it fixes the future timelike vector e_0 (a Lorentz map maps the cone containing e_0 to itself, by lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure(iv)); products of proper orthochronous Lorentz maps are proper orthochronous by the same lemma. (iv) Apply both sides of B(-beta_1)Rhat_1 = B(-beta_2)Rhat_2 to e_0: B(-beta_i)e_0 = gamma_i(e_0 + beta_i^sharp), and the coordinate columns gamma_1(e_0 + beta_1) = gamma_2(e_0 + beta_2) force gamma_1 = gamma_2 and beta_1 = beta_2 (compare the time and spatial coordinates); then Rhat_1 = Rhat_2 by invertibility of the common boost, hence R_1 = R_2. (v) If L = B(beta'), then u = L e_0 = gamma'(e_0 - beta'), so beta = u_vec/u^0 = -beta' and B(beta) = B(-beta'), giving Rhat = B(beta)B(beta') = identity and R = identity; conversely if R = identity then L = B(-beta). No step uses an unstated classification of Lorentz maps; the proof is the finite computation above plus the cited predecessor items.

items.title: The proper orthochronous Lorentz group: boosts, rotations, unique factorization and invariants
items.statement: Let (V,eta) be the Lorentz vector space with time orientation C^+ and let (o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3) be an inertial frame of the model. Then: (i) For every beta in R^3 with |beta| < 1 the passive boost B(beta) is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, B(beta)^{-1} = B(-beta), and for collinear boosts B(beta_1 e)B(beta_2 e) = B(((beta_1 + beta_2)/(1 + beta_1 beta_2)) e) for every unit spatial vector e and beta_1, beta_2 in (-1,1); in particular collinear boosts commute. For each fixed unit spatial axis e and scalar b in (-1,1), the collinear boost B(b e) has b = tanh r for a unique scalar rapidity r in R; rapidities add for boosts along that same fixed axis. This signed scalar rapidity statement does not identify a vector beta in R^3 with the scalar tanh r. (ii) SO^+(V,eta) is a subgroup of O(V,eta), which is a subgroup of GL(V); every passive boost B(beta) and every spatial rotation of the frame (extended by fixing e_0) belongs to SO^+(V,eta). (iii) Every L in SO^+(V,eta) has a unique factorization L = B(-beta) Rhat with |beta| < 1 and Rhat the extension of a spatial rotation of the frame; here beta = u_vec/u^0 where (u^0,u_vec) are the coordinates of u = L e_0. Consequently every proper orthochronous Lorentz map is the product of a passive boost and a spatial rotation (in that order), and L is itself a passive boost if and only if the rotation is the identity. (iv) Every L in SO^+(V,eta) preserves the interval eta(v,v), the causal classification of every nonzero vector, the future and past closed cones, the orientation and the oriented volume form of the model: epsilon(Lv_0,...,Lv_3) = epsilon(v_0,...,v_3) for all v_0,...,v_3 in V. An arbitrary element L of O(V,eta) has det L = +-1 and either preserves or interchanges the future and past cones, and det L = 1 alone does not force L(C^+) = C^+.
items.strategy: Assembly of the page's proved lemmas, with each clause assigned to its supplier. (i) is lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse plus lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition plus the fixed-axis scalar bijection r |-> tanh r of lem-rapidity-parametrization-of-collinear-boosts. The vector boost claims use vector beta; only B(b e) with a specified unit axis uses signed scalar b and r. (ii) is lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure(ii) for the subgroup statements; boosts lie in SO^+(V,eta) by (i), and a spatial rotation Rhat is a Lorentz map fixing the future timelike vector e_0, hence proper of determinant one and orthochronous by lem-boost-rotation-factorization(iii). (iii) is lem-boost-rotation-factorization(ii),(iv),(v). (iv) combines lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure(iii),(iv) with det-preservation; the final sentence records that properness (determinant1) does not imply orthochrony and is witnessed by the B-page counterexample cex-sr-discrete-lorentz-maps-are-not-proper-orthochronous, whose claim is the explicit matrix computation, not an input here. The proof contract must restate the hypotheses (frame fixed, |beta| < 1, L proper orthochronous) and cite each lemma as the whole content of its clause; no clause may be asserted without the corresponding cited result.
