items.title: The uniformly charged ball: interior and exterior fields, continuous potential and finite energy
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $a>0$, $Q\in\mathbb R$, let $\overline B_a=\{x:|x|\le a\}$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and define, with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] ([[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]]),
$$\rho(x):=\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\,\mathbf 1_{\{|x|<a\}}(x),\qquad
E(x):=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\begin{cases}x/a^3,&|x|<a,\\ x/|x|^3,&|x|\ge a,\end{cases}\qquad
\varphi(x):=\begin{cases}\dfrac{Q(3a^2-|x|^2)}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3},&|x|\le a,\\[6pt]\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|},&|x|\ge a.\end{cases}$$
(The value of $\rho$ on the sphere $\{|x|=a\}$ is immaterial: it is a Lebesgue-null set by the polar calculation $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$, since the one-dimensional singleton has measure zero ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]], [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]]).) Then:
(a) [Regularity and gradient] $E$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, of class $C^\infty$ on each of the open regions $\{|x|<a\}$, $\{|x|>a\}$; $\varphi\in C^1(\mathbb R^3)$, its displayed branch derivatives agree on $\{|x|=a\}$, and $E=-\nabla\varphi$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]]);
(b) [Classical equations] for every $x$ with $|x|\ne a$,
$$\operatorname{div}E(x)=\rho(x)/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E(x)=0$$
([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]);
(c) [Weak equations] the pair $(E,(\rho,0))$ satisfies the spatial distributional equations $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$: $E$ is $C^1$ on each side of the sphere $S_a=\{|x|=a\}$ with one-sided smooth extensions near the sphere (the interior affine formula and the exterior formula on $|x|>a/2$), whose values agree, $[E]=0$. Their derivatives are bounded on compact half-neighbourhoods, so the regular-L1 specialization of [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] gives
$$\operatorname{div}E=\{\operatorname{div}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[E]\,\delta_{S_a}=0,$$
with $\rho$ the displayed locally integrable density and no surface-charge term ([[def-em-weak-sources]], [[lem-em-euclidean-balls-and-annuli-are-bounded-c-one-domains]] for the sphere as a compact embedded smooth hypersurface); by the fixed-time reading of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e) these are the weak equations of the static model for this source, with zero singular part;
(d) [Energy] the field energy is finite and equals the assembly integral,
$$\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|E|^2\,d\lambda_3=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\rho\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a},$$
computed with the polar formula ([[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]], [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]); the value agrees with the smooth-source identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] although the density here is only piecewise continuous;
(e) [Consistency and contrast] for $|x|>a$ the field is exactly the point-charge Coulomb field of total charge $Q$ centred at the origin ([[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) with $x_0=0$) although the source is the extended ball, and for $|x|<a$ it is the affine field $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$; $\varphi$ is continuous at $|x|=a$ and decays at infinity; the field is bounded on $\mathbb R^3$, so no divergence of field energy occurs for the extended source;
(f) [Scope] the example verifies the displayed candidate and its energy; it does not claim uniqueness of the solution (this would require boundary data and an infinity condition, and the density is not continuous), it asserts no empirical content, and the density $\rho$ is treated as a bounded $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ density with the sphere carrying no surface charge ($[E]=0$).
items.strategy:
For (a): on $\{|x|<a\}$, $E$ is the affine map $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$ and on $\{|x|>a\}$ it is $Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$; both are $C^\infty$ on their open domains ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[lem-derivative-of-a-power]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]). At $|x|=a$ the two formulas coincide ($x/a^3=x/a^3$), so $E$ is continuous on all of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]], [[def-metric-ball]]). For $\varphi$, the interior branch has gradient $-Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)$ and the exterior branch has gradient $-Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3)$ by the chain rule, and the two gradients agree on $\{|x|=a\}$; the matching derivatives also exist on the interface, as follows. Let $F(r)$ be the displayed radial potential profile on $r\ge0$. Its two branches agree at $a$, and their one-sided derivatives both equal $-Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$, so the difference quotient $(F(a+h)-F(a))/h$ has that common limit from either sign. Thus $F$ is differentiable at $a$, and its derivative is continuous there by the branch formulas. Since $x\mapsto|x|$ is differentiable near each point of $S_a$, the chain rule proves actual total differentiability of $\varphi=F(|x|)$ there and gives the matching gradient. At the origin the interior polynomial already gives smoothness. The resulting partial derivatives exist and are continuous everywhere, whence $\varphi$ is $C^1$ with $\nabla\varphi=-E$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
For (b): inside, $\operatorname{div}(Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3))=3Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3)=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ and the curl of an affine field vanishes ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]); outside, $\operatorname{div}(Qx/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^3))=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_i\partial_i(x_i|x|^{-3})=\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}(3|x|^{-3}-3|x|^{-3})=0$ and the curl components $\partial_j(x_k|x|^{-3})-\partial_k(x_j|x|^{-3})=0$ vanish by the same direct differentiation ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]), matching $\rho=0$ outside.
For (c): the set $S_a$ is a compact embedded smooth hypersurface with unit normal $n=x/|x|$, and the two sides $\Omega_-=\{|x|<a\}$, $\Omega_+=\{|x|>a\}$ are open; $E$ is $C^1$ on each side and its one-sided traces agree on $S_a$ (from (a)), so $[E]=F_+-F_-=0$ in the notation of [[def-em-surface-distribution]] and [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] applies: the distributional divergence is the piecewise classical divergence plus $n\cdot[E]\delta_{S_a}=0$, and the distributional curl is the piecewise classical curl plus $n\times[E]\delta_{S_a}=0$. By (b) the piecewise divergence is $\rho/\varepsilon_0$ as a locally integrable function and the piecewise curl is $0$; the sphere is null by applying [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] to its Borel indicator: $\lambda_3(S_a)=4\pi\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\}}(r)r^2dr=0$. A singleton is contained in intervals of arbitrarily small length, so its one-dimensional measure is zero; [[cor-integral-over-a-null-set-vanishes]] then applies, and the pairing conventions are those of [[def-distribution]], [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. The static reading is [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] (e), and the source objects are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]] with zero singular part.
For (d): by the polar formula and $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ ([[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]], [[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]]) one has $\int_{B_a}|x|^2\,d\lambda_3=4\pi\int_0^ar^4\,dr=\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}$ and $\int_{B_a}d\lambda_3=\frac{4\pi a^3}{3}$; hence
$$\int_{B_a}|E|^2=\Bigl(\frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}\Bigr)^2\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}=\frac{Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0^2a},\qquad \int_{|x|>a}|E|^2=\frac{Q^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2}\cdot 4\pi\int_a^\infty r^{-2}dr=\frac{Q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0^2a},$$
using $\int_a^\infty r^{-2}dr=1/a$ ([[thm-ftc-second-part]] and monotone convergence, [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]], [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); the sum times $\varepsilon_0/2$ is $\frac{Q^2}{40\pi\varepsilon_0a}+\frac{Q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a}=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$. The assembly integral is computed from the same two radial integrals, $\frac12\int\rho\varphi=\frac12\frac{3Q}{4\pi a^3}\frac{Q}{8\pi\varepsilon_0a^3}\bigl(3a^2\frac{4\pi a^3}{3}-\frac{4\pi a^5}{5}\bigr)=\frac{3Q^2}{20\pi\varepsilon_0a}$, so the identity of [[pthm-em-electrostatic-field-energy]] extends to this piecewise-continuous bounded density by direct verification; the density is bounded with compact support and all integrands are continuous off a null sphere ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[cor-continuous-functions-are-borel-measurable]]).
For (e): the exterior branch equals the formula of [[pthm-em-coulomb-solution]] (d) with $q=Q$, $x_0=0$; $\varphi$ is continuous at $|x|=a$ since both branches give $Q/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a)$, and decays like $1/|x|$; $|E|\le |Q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0a^2)$ on $\mathbb R^3$, so the energy of (d) is finite and no point singularity arises. For (f): no uniqueness or empirical statement is used anywhere; the sphere's zero jump is exactly the checked equality of the two branches on $\{|x|=a\}$. The one-dimensional singleton used in the polar null-sphere calculation is null by [[prop-degenerate-boxes-and-coordinate-hyperplanes-are-lebesgue-null]]. Finite-interval integrations of the continuous one-variable test/radial integrands above use [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]] to identify their Riemann/FTC values with their Lebesgue values before Fubini, polar integration or passage to improper limits; real and imaginary test components are treated separately. In(c), regular bulk is justified by the actual formulas, not agreement of value traces alone. The affine formula extends smoothly across the inner side of S_a and x/|x|^3 extends smoothly across its outer side on |x|>a/2. Their first derivatives are bounded near each compact sphere patch, so piecewise derivatives are locally integrable; this is the regular specialization of the repaired interface lemma. The zero jump and every field/energy formula remain unchanged.

items.physical_scope: The uniformly charged ball of radius $a$ and total charge $Q$ in vacuum: the candidate piecewise field and continuous potential, the pointwise and distributional static equations with the piecewise-constant density and zero surface charge, the exterior Coulomb field of total charge $Q$, the vanishing jump of the normal field, and the finite energy $3Q^2/(20\pi\varepsilon_0a)$ equal to the assembly integral. items.title: Declared averaging kernel, macroscopic scale assumptions and averaged fields
items.statement:
Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following coarse-graining convention for matter. Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields and its sources be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis of the smoothing theorem cited in clause (b).
(a) [Averaging length, kernel and footprint] Fix $\ell>0$ and nonnegative $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\int\eta=1$, in the Euclidean test-function convention of def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions. Put $\eta_\ell(x)=\ell^{-3}\eta(x/\ell)$, $K=\operatorname{supp}\eta$ and choose a declared finite bound $R_\eta>0$ with $K\subseteq\overline B_{R_\eta}(0)$. The kernel and length are fixed data; the imported mass-one mollifier definition does not require $K\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$. At x the exact averaging footprint is $x-\ell K$. Define the open interior averaging domain $$\Omega_{\ell,\eta}:=\{x\in\Omega:x-\ell K\subseteq\Omega\}.$$ The sufficient condition $\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega)>\ell R_\eta$ implies membership. If the additional unit-support condition $K\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$ is declared, the original sufficient region $\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^3\setminus\Omega)>\ell$ and the ball $B_\ell(x)$ are valid special cases; unit support is not inferred from mass one.
(b) [Averaged fields and input regularity] For an open spatial domain V, locally integrable means measurable and absolutely integrable on every compact subset of V, componentwise for maps to $\mathbb R^m$, $m=1$ or 3. First suppose $F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$ has a locally integrable spatial slice $F(\cdot,t)$ for every t under consideration. No integrability across the boundary of Omega is required for the interior branch. Define, for $x\in\Omega_{\ell,\eta}$, $$F_\ell(x,t)=\int_\Omega\eta_\ell(x-y)F(y,t)dy.$$ The compact footprint lies in Omega, so this integral exists absolutely, and for each such t it is smooth in x on $\Omega_{\ell,\eta}$ with $$\partial_x^\alpha F_\ell(x,t)=\int_\Omega(\partial^\alpha\eta_\ell)(x-y)F(y,t)dy$$ for every multi-index. These are applications of the pinned mollifier smoothing supplier after a local compact cutoff, not an assumption that zero extension across the original boundary is locally integrable. For each admissible fixed t the spatial convolution is measurable in x and independent of a.e.-equal spatial representatives; no joint (x,t) measurability follows from the every-slice hypothesis alone. Joint $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega\times I)$ input alone instead gives these slice statements for almost every t, by local Fubini on compact spatial/time exhaustions; it gives no every-time slice claim. A claim for every t must explicitly supply locally integrable slices for every t (for example jointly continuous fields supply that condition). A spacetime a.e. class alone determines the resulting averages only for almost every t; changing an exceptional time slice may change its pointwise-time assignment. Spatial smoothing asserts no time differentiability or joint smoothness without separately stated time hypotheses.
[Compatible extension branch] If a declared extension $\widehat F(\cdot,t)$ agrees with F a.e. on Omega and is locally integrable on an open larger spatial domain V, use the same formula there for all x whose compact footprint lies in V. If $V=\mathbb R^3$ and every declared slice is globally locally integrable, the average is defined and spatially smooth on all $\mathbb R^3\times I$. If only joint local integrability of the extension is supplied, the global spatial conclusion is for almost every t unless the every-slice hypothesis is added. The zero extension is an allowed choice only when it meets this local-integrability condition: equivalently, at each declared t, $\int_{Q\cap\Omega}|F(y,t)|dy<\infty$ for every compact $Q\subset\mathbb R^3$. Mere local integrability inside Omega does not imply that boundary condition. All these extension and per-time conditions are part of the declared configuration, with the original interior branch retaining every locally integrable spatial input.
(c) [Macroscopic reading and scale separation] The framework reads its macroscopic fields and source densities as such averages only in situations where a separation of microscopic and observation scales is stated for the problem at hand; the averaging length and the actual kernel footprint (or its radius bound $\ell R_\eta$) are part of that statement, and no canonical value of $\ell$ is asserted. This is a formulation choice for the macroscopic description, not a consequence of the vacuum equations.
(d) [Boundary handling] For requested averages at $x\in\Omega$, boundary handling concerns the locations where $x-\ell K$ is not contained in the original spatial domain. The region $\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)\le\ell R_\eta\}$ is a sufficient enclosing boundary layer, with $\ell$ in place of $\ell R_\eta$ only in the declared unit-support special case. Every requested average at an exterior location $x\notin\Omega$ must separately satisfy the extension/domain conditions of (b); the interior boundary-layer statement makes no claim to enclose exterior locations. In the interior layer a zero-extension average is used only under the compatible-extension hypothesis of (b). Otherwise one must declare another locally integrable extension, a boundary-layer model with its own well-definedness hypotheses, or restrict the averaging domain to the exact interior footprint domain. No boundary model is supplied by local integrability alone. An extension does not automatically extend a microscopic field equation across the original boundary; any averaging of such equations must either declare their validity on all used extended footprints or retain the resulting boundary distribution terms. These boundary qualifications do not impose a constitutive law.
(e) [No constitutive content] Coarse graining reorganises the description; it does not by itself produce a constitutive relation between averaged fields and averaged sources, and no linear, local or instantaneous response is asserted by this postulate. Such a response is the separate assumption [[post-em-material-closure]], and the derivation of macroscopic field equations from the vacuum equations is the separate result [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]].
items.strategy:
An adopted nonproof formulation: the macroscopic identification and scale-separation/boundary conventions are adopted, not deduced from vacuum Maxwell or asserted empirically. Its mathematical referent is checked against the exact published mollifier contract, which permits any smooth compactly supported mass-one kernel and requires locally integrable input on the region used by its compact translates; it imposes no unit support.

Interior applicability: for x0 in the exact footprint domain, x0-ell K is compact inside Omega. A sufficiently small closed ball of x-values about x0 has all its translated kernel supports in one compact Q contained in Omega. This follows from compactness and openness, and proves the footprint domain open. At each admissible t let f_Q be F(.,t) on Q and zero elsewhere. Since Q is compact inside Omega, f_Q belongs to global L1 and hence L1loc. The published mollifier smoothing theorem applied to f_Q gives a smooth convolution and every derivative by differentiating the kernel. In that small x-neighbourhood it equals the declared interior integral, and every derivative has support inside Q as well. This proves absolute existence, spatial smoothness and the derivative formula for arbitrary interior L1loc data. Spatial a.e. representatives give equal integrals for each x because translated kernel weights are bounded and have compact support. Compactness of K gives its finite support-radius bound; no equality to 1 is assumed.

Slice qualification: exhaust Omega by compact sets K_j={x:|x|<=j,dist(x,R3 minus Omega)>=1/j} (use the usual convention if Omega=R3), and the open laboratory interval by compact subintervals. On each compact product joint local integrability makes F absolutely integrable. Apply the L1 Fubini theorem to these compact restrictions extended by zero to the Euclidean product. Outside a null exceptional time set the spatial integrals on each K_j are finite; a countable union of these exceptional sets is null under the already declared countable-choice convention. Thus a.e. time slices are locally integrable, because every compact subset of Omega lies in some K_j. It does not prove every-time slices or uniquely determine assignments at exceptional times. No time derivative is inferred. The compatible-extension branch uses the same precise supplier with its hypotheses checked on the declared larger domain; the all-space branch applies only when the extension is globally L1loc per slice. Zero extension has that property exactly when its absolute integral on Q equals the finite integral over Q intersect Omega for every global compact Q. A field such as 1/x1 on x1>0 fails this condition, so no unconditional boundary extension is asserted.

The enclosing boundary-layer claim is restricted to x inside Omega; requested exterior averages are governed separately by the footprint/extension conditions. Measurability in the every-slice branch refers to x at each admissible fixed t, with no unassumed joint measurability. Clauses (c)-(e) retain the adopted macroscopic reading, require the actual kernel footprint in scale separation, and distinguish smoothing from constitutive closure and field equations. No deductive proof of this modelling postulate is supplied or claimed. These local applicability arguments and inherited mathematical supplier pins are not independent source/audit acceptance.

items.title: Polarization, magnetization, bound and free sources, and the fields D and H
items.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its units, its fields $E,B$ and its source densities $\rho,J$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-sources]], and let the averaging convention be that of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], in whose sense the objects below are macroscopic. Any convolution used to instantiate that reading is taken on its declared exact interior-footprint domain, or under a declared locally integrable compatible extension covering every used footprint. Its every-time use requires every-time locally integrable spatial slices; joint spacetime local integrability alone supplies only the almost-every-time branch. The joint C2 regularity specified below is a separate model hypothesis, not a consequence of spatial smoothing.
(a) [Polarization and magnetization] The material model specifies two maps $P,M:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] on the open set $\Omega\times I$: $P$ is the electric dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, and $M$ the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume, in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, both read in the frame basis. They are data of the chosen material model: this definition does not compute them from $E$ and $B$, and no relation between $(P,M)$ and the fields is asserted here.
(b) [Bound sources] Write $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ for the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] taken at fixed $t$, and $\partial_t$ for the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] at fixed position, and define the bound charge density and bound current density by $$\rho_b:=-\operatorname{div}P,\qquad J_b:=\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M.$$ Since $P,M$ are jointly $C^2$, $\rho_b$ and $J_b$ are continuous (indeed $C^1$); $\rho_b$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J_b$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.
(c) [Free sources] Define $\rho_f:=\rho-\rho_b$ and $J_f:=J-J_b$, in the same units as $\rho$ and $J$; these are the free charge and free current densities of the model. The decomposition $\rho=\rho_f+\rho_b$, $J=J_f+J_b$ is part of the chosen material model: the same total pair $(\rho,J)$ with a different pair $(P,M)$ is a different model.
(d) [Displacement and magnetic intensity] Define the electric displacement and the magnetic intensity by $$D:=\varepsilon_0E+P,\qquad H:=\mu_0^{-1}B-M,$$ where $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and $\mu_0,c>0$ are the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; $D$ carries $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$ and $H$ carries $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-1}$.
(e) [Status] This item fixes objects and the bound/free convention only. No field equation ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]), no constitutive relation ([[post-em-material-closure]]), no conservation of the bound pair ([[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]](a)) and no identification of $P,M$ with microscopic dipole sums is asserted here.
items.strategy: An explicit type/domain/convention definition. The regions, fields and sources are those of the named suppliers; the derivatives in (b) are the published divergence, curl and partial derivative; the constants and units are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the $C^2$ class is that of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; the macroscopic reading is the convention of [[post-em-coarse-graining]], with its actual footprint/compatible-extension and slice hypotheses carried whenever convolution is used. Joint C2 regularity of the model maps is assumed separately; the spatial averaging operation proves neither time differentiability nor the existence of microscopic dipole sums. The definition records explicitly that $(P,M)$ are model data read in the laboratory frame basis, that the bound/free split is a modelling choice, and that no constitutive relation between $(P,M)$ and $(E,B)$ is included. Well-definedness of $\rho_b,J_b$ as continuous fields is the componentwise sum/product differentiability calculus of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. No field equation, no derivative of the physical fields and no microscopic interpretation is used.

items.title: The macroscopic Maxwell equations in terms of D, H and the free sources
items.statement:
Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]: fields $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ jointly of class $C^1$ with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and continuous source densities $\rho,J$ of [[def-em-sources]]. Let $P,M$ and the derived objects $\rho_b,J_b,\rho_f,J_f,D,H$ be those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]], with $P,M$ of class $C^2$, and use the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:
(a) [Bound-source conservation] $\partial_t\rho_b+\operatorname{div}J_b=0$ on $\Omega\times I$. Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the regular-distribution and classical-compatibility interfaces below. Identify continuous sources with their regular distributions using [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]] and [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]. Then $$\partial_t\rho_f+\operatorname{div}J_f=\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J$$ as distributions on $U$, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]: the free pair is distributionally conserved exactly when the total pair is. Under the adopted four vacuum equations both sides are zero distributions, by [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]. These statements do not require classical derivatives of $\rho,J$. Where the partial derivatives $\partial_t\rho$ and $\partial_{x_i}J_i$ exist, the same identity holds pointwise by differentiating the free/bound decomposition; in particular, if these derivatives are continuous on $U$, both pairs satisfy the classical pointwise continuity equation. The bound-source conservation equation remains classical and uses only $P,M\in C^2$.
(b) [Macroscopic equations] On $\Omega\times I$, $$\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD.$$
(c) [Interpretation and scope] Equations (b) are an exact rewriting of the adopted vacuum equations under the decomposition of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]: the two equations written in $E$ and $B$ are unchanged, and the $D$ and $H$ equations hold for every $C^2$ pair $(P,M)$, independently of any constitutive law. The classical bound identity of (a) uses the exchange of $\partial_t$ with $\operatorname{div}$ for $C^2$ data; the free/total identity is distributional in the stated continuous-source class, with its classical interpretation only under the additional derivatives stated in (a). The distributional conservation conclusion embeds the adopted smooth solution only; no macroscopic field-equation claim is made for the weak branch of the Maxwell postulate, for singular or sheet sources or for discontinuous $(P,M)$; no constitutive relation and no empirical statement is made.
items.strategy: **Proof technique:** direct substitution, componentwise. (a): from [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]](b), $\operatorname{div}J_b=\operatorname{div}\partial_tP+\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M$. The second term vanishes: in components $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}M=\sum_{i,j,k=1}^3\epsilon_{ijk}\partial_i\partial_jM_k$, and pairwise cancellation of the mixed partials $\partial_i\partial_jM_k=\partial_j\partial_iM_k$ is [[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]] applied to the $C^2$ components of $M$; the first term equals $\partial_t\operatorname{div}P$ by the same theorem applied to the $C^2$ components of $P$; adding $-\partial_t\operatorname{div}P$ gives zero. Linearity of $\partial_t$, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ is [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] read componentwise. (b): Gauss's law $\operatorname{div}E=(\rho_f+\rho_b)/\varepsilon_0$ together with $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ gives $\operatorname{div}(\varepsilon_0E+P)=\rho_f$, i.e. $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$. The equations $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ are unchanged. Ampere's law $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$ with $J=J_f+\partial_tP+\operatorname{curl}M$ gives, after dividing by $\mu_0$ and moving $\operatorname{curl}M$ to the left, $\operatorname{curl}(\mu_0^{-1}B-M)=J_f+\partial_tP+\varepsilon_0\partial_tE$, where $(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}=\varepsilon_0$; the right-hand side is $J_f+\partial_t(\varepsilon_0E+P)=J_f+\partial_tD$, so $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$. (c) records the scope: the identities are conditional on the adopted postulates and on $P,M\in C^2$; no constitutive content is used. For the free/total identity, subtract the regular distributions of the classical bound pair from those of the continuous total pair and differentiate linearly. Under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]] identifies the $C^1$ bound derivatives with their classical regular distributions, so their sum is zero; this proves the distributional identity without differentiating the merely continuous total sources classically. Embed the four adopted $C^1$ Maxwell equations and apply spatial divergence to Ampere: commuting distributional derivatives cancels $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}B$ and Gauss gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$. If the displayed source derivatives exist, linearity gives the pointwise free/total identity; if they are continuous, classical compatibility and injectivity of the regular-distribution embedding give pointwise zero. Only the regular-distribution/classical-compatibility branch invokes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$; the classical bound calculation and the macroscopic substitution in (b) remain choice-free.

Free/total conservation is distributional for the continuous-source class under AC_omega, and classical under the stated additional source derivatives.

items.title: Declared material-closure branches: linear nondispersive Ohmic response and the causal memory branch
items.statement:
Adopt as a modelling postulate of this framework the following constitutive branches for the material described by the macroscopic fields of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]].
(a) [Material rest frame] The relations below are stated in a material rest frame: an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the Minkowski model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) in which the material element under consideration is at rest, with spatial basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$; when the material is at rest in the laboratory frame of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the components below are the laboratory components. Boosting the material changes both the fields and the rest observer; this postulate does not assert that the relations below hold with the same constants in every frame.
(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch] In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes $$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$ where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$; local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.
(c) [Causal memory branch] Alternatively, and again in the rest frame, the polarisation response to the electric history is the causal convolution $$P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)\,E(t-s)\,ds$$ for a declared real matrix kernel $K:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ in $L^1(0,\infty)$ ([[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]); the integral then converges absolutely for bounded continuous histories $E$ because $|K_{jk}(s)E_k(t-s)|\le(\sup|E_k|)|K_{jk}(s)|$. The kernel class actually used, together with causality and passivity, is part of the model and is analysed in [[pthm-em-causal-dispersive-response]]; neither causality nor passivity is automatic. A finitely-subtracted analytic response may instead be declared by a scalar transfer function $\chi$ that is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, of class $C^1$ on the real boundary away from a real subtraction point $\omega_0$, holomorphic on a neighbourhood of $\omega_0$, and satisfies $|\chi(z)|\le C(1+|z|^{n-1})$ on $\{\operatorname{Im}z\ge0\}$ outside a compact set for some integer $n\ge1$ and constant $C>0$ ([[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]]).
(d) [Status] These are adopted model assumptions, one branch at a time; the framework does not derive them from the vacuum equations or from coarse graining, and no microscopic mechanism, material data or empirical validity is claimed. Ferroelectric and ferromagnetic response, hysteresis, nonlinear response and general nonlocal response lie outside the branches declared here.
items.strategy: An adopted nonproof formulation. The objects are those of [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]]; the macroscopic field equations whose formulation the closure completes are those of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; the rest-frame notion is the inertial frame of [[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]] used by [[def-em-lab-geometry]], and the memory-branch kernel class is the $L^1$ notion of [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]], whose absolute convergence for bounded continuous histories is the elementary domination displayed in the statement. The finitely-subtracted branch uses the holomorphy notion of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]] and states its growth and boundary hypotheses explicitly rather than hiding them. Clause (d) records that the branches are assumptions with no microscopic or empirical content. No proof is supplied and none is claimed, in accordance with the nonproof status of a postulate; the source and scope review covers the formulation, the rest-frame and scale qualifications and the non-derivation.

items.title: Stationary macroscopic interface jump conditions for D, B, E and H
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), the hypothesis under which [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] and the surface conventions of [[def-em-weak-sources]] are stated, and let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]]), let $\sigma_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K_f:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous with $K_f(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$ (a free surface charge density and a tangential free surface current density, both stationary in $t$), and let $\rho_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $J_v:(\Omega\setminus S)\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$. Let $E,B,D,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be locally integrable on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ on $(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$, with the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension property: around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side of each field is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder, so that the fields and their first space and time derivatives extend continuously to that side, locally uniformly on compact cylinders. Write $[F]=F_+-F_-$ for the jump of the one-sided traces.
[Thin-interface hypothesis] Suppose that $E,B,D,H$ satisfy the four macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the distributional sense on $U$ with the source pair $\rho_f=\rho_v+\sigma_f\delta_S$, $J_f=J_v+K_f\delta_S$, where the stationary-sheet pairings are those of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c) and the equations are $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ as identities in the sense of [[def-distribution]], the fields being identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $\psi$ ranging over $C_c^\infty(U)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]). This thin-interface solution hypothesis is a modelling assumption of the statement: it is the natural weakening of the smooth macroscopic equations to fields with a common stationary discontinuity, and it is not deduced from the smooth-region equations alone.
Then, pointwise on $S\times I$, $$n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f,\qquad n\cdot[B]=0,\qquad n\times[E]=0,\qquad n\times[H]=K_f,$$ with the Euclidean inner and cross products of the one-sided traces ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); equivalently $\sigma_f=n\cdot[D]$ and $K_f=n\times[H]$ recover the free sheet densities from the field jumps.
[Weak-trace branch] If instead of the joint extension hypothesis the fields have the original one-sided spatial $C^1$ extensions at each time and, in addition, the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the one-sided field traces are measurable and locally integrable on $S\times I$ with respect to $dS\,dt$, then the same four identities hold as identities of sheet distributions and for $dS\,dt$-almost every $(x,t)$; since the traces are spatially continuous at each fixed time, they hold for every $x\in S$ for almost every $t$, and at every $(x,t)$ whenever the jump densities are additionally jointly continuous. Merely having one-sided spatial $C^1$ traces separately at every time does not justify the last upgrade.
[Scope] In the joint one-sided spacetime $C^1$ extension branch, stationarity and the joint extensions make $\partial_tD$ and $\partial_tB$ locally bounded near $S$ and hence locally integrable, contributing no delta terms. In the weak-trace branch the explicitly assumed locally integrable temporal derivatives provide this conclusion instead. No magnetic charge and no magnetic surface current are present in the sources; no dipolar sheet layer (a concentrated dipole distribution in $P$ or $M$, which would make the fields non-integrable) is included. No existence theorem for fields with singular sources is asserted, no constitutive law is used, and no empirical claim is made. In this weak branch temporal derivatives in $L^1_{\rm loc}$ are genuine weak derivatives, or classical derivatives with the joint interior $C^1$ integration-by-parts justification already assumed. More generally, that temporal integrability hypothesis may be omitted when the stated spatial derivative and trace integrability and the actual fixed-sheet weak equations with regular volume sources hold: those equations themselves imply the same jumps and regular temporal derivatives. No joint boundary continuity is imposed on this broader branch.
items.strategy: **Proof technique:** apply [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] to the four fields and match the coefficients of the surface distribution. By [[lem-em-interface-derivatives]] ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ declared), for $C^1$-off-$S$ fields with one-sided $C^1$ traces, $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\cdot[D]\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[H]\,\delta_S$, with the analogous identities for $B$ and $E$. Substituting into the distributional identities of the hypothesis and using the sheet pairings of [[def-em-weak-sources]](c), the regular parts reproduce the off-interface macroscopic equations and the coefficients of $\delta_S$ give, one equation at a time, $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ (from $\operatorname{div}D=\rho_f$), $n\cdot[B]=0$ (from $\operatorname{div}B=0$), $n\times[E]=0$ and $n\times[H]=K_f$: the right-hand sides $\partial_tB$ and $J_f+\partial_tD$ carry no delta term because $S$ is stationary and the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis makes $\partial_tB$ and $\partial_tD$ locally bounded near $S$, hence locally integrable. Since the two-sided traces are continuous on $S\times I$, the distributional coefficient identities are the displayed pointwise identities. The weak-trace branch replaces the pointwise trace argument by the $dS\,dt$-almost-everywhere sheet identity plus the spatial-continuity upgrade. No constitutive relation and no field equation beyond the assumed distributional identities is used. To justify the broader weak branch directly, first apply the regular-L1 specialization of the spatial interface lemma at each admissible time and integrate by Fubini. Its spatial distributional sheet coefficient is the stated trace jump. Work on a compact graph patch with a smooth tube cutoff chi_epsilon(y), independent of time, equal to one on the sheet, bounded between zero and one, and supported where |z-g(y)|<2epsilon; multiply by a fixed compact test. This cutoff need only be C2 for a C2 graph: all equations involved are order at most one. To use it legitimately, approximate the resulting compactly supported C1 test in the C1 norm by smooth tests via [[thm-convolution-with-a-mollifier-is-smooth-and-differentiates-under-the-integral-sign]], using its actual kernel-footprint margin. For each derivative of order at most one, move the derivative to the compact C1 input by classical integration by parts and write the error as integral eta(v)[D^alpha f(x-epsilon v)-D^alpha f(x)]dv. Uniform continuity on one compact enlarged support and the finite integral of |eta| make this error uniformly vanish; no unit-support assumption is made. The L1 and finite sheet measures make all pairings continuous in that norm, so the weak identities extend to it. For a temporal term its absolute pairing is at most the integral over the shrinking spatial tube of |F| times the fixed time-derivative bound. For a regular spatial bulk or volume source use its absolute L1 majorant. The sheet has ambient volume zero, and [[thm-dominated-convergence]] sends all these integrals to zero. The sheet term survives unchanged because chi_epsilon=1 on S. Thus the four weak equations force exactly their four displayed sheet coefficients, without assuming a temporal classical derivative is integrable or demanding joint continuous boundary values. After cancelling these coefficients, the curl evolution equations identify the weak temporal derivatives with their regular spatial bulk and volume-source expressions, which are L1loc. The existing scalar-test localization and Countable Choice a.e.-time argument then give the stated sheet-a.e., spatial-continuity and joint-continuity upgrades. The original jointly C1 interior branch is included and supports its classical temporal integration by parts; the general given-L1 Maxwell admission stays unrestricted.

items.title: Specified causal material response: transfer function, dispersion relations and the passivity condition
items.statement:
Assume the memory branch of the material-closure postulate [[post-em-material-closure]] in a material rest frame, and assume the hypotheses of the mathematical suppliers [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] and [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]]: Countable Choice for the smooth comparison route and, in the integrable branches, Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]]). Let $E:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the electric-field history in the material rest frame, read componentwise in its spatial basis ([[def-em-fields]]), and let $P$ be the polarisation response declared by the model.
(a) [Causal response] If the kernel of [[post-em-material-closure]](c) satisfies $K\in L^1(0,\infty;\mathbb R^{3\times3})$, then for every bounded continuous history $E$ the response $P(t)=\varepsilon_0\int_0^\infty K(s)E(t-s)\,ds$ is well defined for every $t$, bounded and continuous, linear in $E$, and causal: histories equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$ produce responses equal on $(-\infty,t_0]$.
(b) [Transfer function and dispersion relations] If $K$ is smooth with compact support in $(0,\infty)$, the transfer function $\chi(z)=\int_0^\infty K(s)e^{izs}\,ds$ is entire, satisfies $\chi(-\omega)=\overline{\chi(\omega)}$ for real $\omega$, obeys $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le\|K_{jk}''\|_{L^1}|z|^{-2}$ for $z\ne0$ with $\operatorname{Im}z\ge0$ (with the whole-plane bound carrying the exponential factor $e^{b\max(0,-\operatorname{Im}z)}$ when $\operatorname{supp}K\subseteq(0,b)$), and its entries satisfy the principal-value dispersion relations of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]](b). If $K$ is locally absolutely continuous on $[0,\infty)$ with $K,K'\in L^1$ and $sK\in L^1$, then $\chi$ is holomorphic on the open upper half-plane, continuous with continuous first derivative on the real boundary, obeys the stated growth bound, and satisfies the same pair of relations; an instantaneous real part $\chi_\infty$ may be added to the model, and the relations apply to $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}-\chi_\infty$ for $\chi_{\mathrm{total}}=\chi_\infty+\chi$.
(c) [Finitely-subtracted and polynomial branches] For each specified integer $n\ge1$ for which the full hypotheses of [[lem-em-finitely-subtracted-analytic-dispersion]] hold for the declared response transfer function, its $n$-subtracted relations apply entrywise. These hypotheses include upper-half-plane holomorphy, continuity on the closed upper half-plane, the stated boundary $C^1$ regularity, holomorphy near the real subtraction point $\omega_0$, and the order-specific growth bound $|\chi_{jk}(z)|\le C_{jk}(1+|z|^{n-1})$ outside a compact set. The Taylor polynomial and residual are
$$P_n(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{\chi^{(j)}(\omega_0)}{j!}(z-\omega_0)^j,\qquad f_n(z)=\frac{\chi(z)-P_n(z)}{(z-\omega_0)^n},$$
with removable values and the boundary $C^1$ hypothesis read entrywise as in the supplier. A growth bound for one order $n_0$ permits every order $n\ge n_0$ under the same local analytic and boundary hypotheses; it does not justify lower orders for which the required growth fails. The unsubtracted $n=0$ case is included only under its own decay and boundary hypotheses: $P_0=0$, $f_0=\chi$, growth $O(1/|z|)$, and factor $(\omega-\omega_0)^0=1$ with the supplier's principal-value convention. The separate constitutive-polynomial branch $\sum_{j=0}^mA_jE^{(j)}+K*E$, with real coefficients or matrices $A_j$ and $K$ satisfying the supplier's integrable causal hypotheses, is causal on histories with bounded continuous derivatives through order $m$. Its transfer is $Q(z)+\chi_K(z)$ with $Q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(-iz)^j$. Subtracting the declared $Q$ leaves the proved relations for $\chi_K$, without assuming that $Q$ is the Taylor polynomial $P_n$.

(d) [Monochromatic work, instantaneous work and passivity] Let $\omega>0$, $e\in\mathbb C^3$ and $E(t)=\operatorname{Re}(e e^{-i\omega t})$. Write $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)$ for the full transfer matrix used in the response: it is $\chi(\omega)$ without an instantaneous term and $\chi_\infty+\chi(\omega)$ when the arbitrary real instantaneous matrix $\chi_\infty\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is present. The period-averaged work per unit volume is
$$\langle E\cdot\partial_tP\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)e).$$
It is nonnegative for every $e$ if and only if the full Hermitian dissipative part
$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)-\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)^*}{2i}$$
is positive semidefinite. This frequencywise monochromatic passivity is an additional model condition, not a consequence of causality or dispersion.

For the instantaneous part set $S=(\chi_\infty+\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$ and $A=(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T})/2$, so $S^{\mathsf T}=S$ and $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$. For any real $C^1$ history its exact instantaneous work split is
$$E\cdot\partial_t(\varepsilon_0\chi_\infty E)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E\cdot S E\right)+\varepsilon_0 E\cdot A\partial_tE.$$
The symmetric part therefore supplies the quadratic storage term; no positivity of that term is asserted unless $S$ is additionally positive semidefinite. The antisymmetric part has $E\cdot A E=0$ but can supply nonzero work over a cycle. Its monochromatic contribution is $\varepsilon_0\omega\operatorname{Im}(e^*A e)/2$, and
$$M_{\mathrm{tot}}(\omega)=M_K(\omega)+A/i,\qquad M_K(\omega)=\frac{\chi(\omega)-\chi(\omega)^*}{2i}.$$
Thus only a symmetric real instantaneous matrix contributes purely this storage term for all histories; for an arbitrary real instantaneous matrix the passivity test must include its antisymmetric contribution. For example, $\chi_\infty=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$, $K=0$ and $e=(1,i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ give $E=(\cos\omega t,\sin\omega t,0)$, zero quadratic storage and averaged work $\varepsilon_0\omega>0$. The opposite circular amplitude $(1,-i,0)^{\mathsf T}$ gives averaged work $-\varepsilon_0\omega$, so this instantaneous response is causal but fails the all-amplitude passivity condition.

(e) [Scope] The response is declared in the material rest frame of [[post-em-material-closure]](a); boosting the material changes the fields and the rest observer, and no frame-independent instantaneous response law is asserted. The framework does not claim that any particular material realises these branches, no microscopic mechanism is derived, and no empirical statement is made.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** supplier identification for the analytic branches, followed by finite-dimensional work calculations.

(a)–(b) Apply the fully stated mathematical response supplier entrywise to the declared rest-frame kernel and multiply its convolution by the framework's positive normalization $\varepsilon_0$. This retains existence, continuity, boundedness, linearity, causality, the stated entire or upper-half-plane analytic transfer, reality identity, decay and dispersion conditions. Adding any real constant matrix changes only the total transfer, and the dispersion formulas remain those for $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}-\chi_\infty$; this analytic subtraction asserts no work or storage property.

(c) Fix an order $n$ satisfying the exact finite-subtraction supplier hypotheses. Taylor expansion near $\omega_0$ makes the zero in $\chi-P_n$ removable after division by $(z-\omega_0)^n$, and the order-specific growth yields $f_n(z)=O(1/|z|)$ in the closed upper half-plane. The supplier's boundary contour proof then gives its two principal-value relations. Do not apply it to a lower order without that order's growth bound. If the bound holds at $n_0$, then $1+|z|^{n_0-1}\le2(1+|z|^{n-1})$ for $|z|\ge1$ and $n\ge n_0$, so the growth bound also holds at every larger order. Local holomorphy near $\omega_0$ supplies all the corresponding Taylor derivatives and removable boundary regularity; away from that point division by a nonzero polynomial preserves the stated $C^1$ boundary property. The distinct $n=0$ branch requires its own decay. For the constitutive polynomial, the derivative multiplier on $e^{-i\omega t}$ is $(-i\omega)^j$, so the declared transfer polynomial is exactly $Q$, and the remainder $\chi_K$ uses the integrable supplier rather than an assumed Taylor identification.

(d) Apply clause (d) of [[thm-em-causal-dispersive-response]] to the whole monochromatic transfer matrix. Its proof uses the finite period-average identity and makes no analytic, decay, symmetry or memory-kernel assumption about that matrix, so it applies equally to $\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}$. The identity $e^*M_{\mathrm{tot}}e=\operatorname{Im}(e^*\chi_{\mathrm{tot}}e)$ proves the exact positive-semidefinite criterion. For arbitrary real $\chi_\infty$, decompose it as $S+A$. The coordinate product rule and symmetry give $\frac{d}{dt}(E^{\mathsf T}SE)=2E^{\mathsf T}S\partial_tE$, whereas $E^{\mathsf T}AE=0$ by transposition. Hence the displayed exact work split. On a periodic history the storage derivative has zero average. Because a real symmetric $S$ is Hermitian, $e^*Se$ is real; the remaining average is the stated antisymmetric quadratic form. The real matrix identity $\chi_\infty^*=\chi_\infty^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(\chi_\infty-\chi_\infty^*)/(2i)=A/i$ and the total dissipative-part formula. In the explicit skew example, $\chi_\infty e=(i,-1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $e^*\chi_\infty e=2i$; directly $\partial_tE=\omega(-\sin\omega t,\cos\omega t,0)$ and $\chi_\infty\partial_tE=\omega E$, giving work $\varepsilon_0\omega$ at every time. Replacing $i$ by $-i$ reverses the work. More generally, if a real antisymmetric matrix has $A_{jk}=a\ne0$, choosing $e=e_j+i e_k$ yields $e^*Ae=2ia$, hence nonzero cycle work. Therefore pure storage for all histories requires $A=0$, while $A=0$ suffices. No sign condition for an arbitrary matrix or positivity of storage is inferred from reality alone.

(e) Retain the material-rest-frame scope, every stated Choice hypothesis and the absence of microscopic or empirical conclusions. These finite-dimensional corrections add no Choice assumption and no material-realization claim.

items.title: Energy balance and Ohmic dissipation for the constant nondispersive linear model
items.statement:
Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]]: constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (isotropic scalar case included) with $D=\varepsilon E$ and $B=\mu H$, and the conduction relation $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ with $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite and a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Assume the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the regularity hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], so that its macroscopic equations hold on $\Omega\times I$. Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector $$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$ with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then:
(a) [Local balance and positivity] On $\Omega\times I$, $$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E.$$ Moreover $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot\varepsilon E+H\cdot\mu H)\ge0$, with $u(x,t)>0$ whenever $(E(x,t),H(x,t))\ne(0,0)$.
(b) [Dissipation reading] With $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $\sigma$ symmetric positive semidefinite, $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ and the balance reads $$\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S+E\cdot\sigma E=-J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E;$$ the nonnegative term $E\cdot\sigma E$ is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.
(c) [Fixed-volume balance] Let $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ be open with $\overline{\Omega'}\subseteq\Omega$ carrying the finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]], let $t_0<t_1$ with $(t_0,t_1)\subseteq I$, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) as in that divergence theorem, and let $n$ be the outward unit normal of $\partial\Omega'$. Then for every $t\in(t_0,t_1)$, $$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u(x,t)\,dx=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E\,dx-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS.$$
(d) [Scope] The density $u=\tfrac12(E\cdot D+B\cdot H)$ is a stored-energy density only for this constant symmetric nondispersive model; for general dispersive, nonlocal, nonlinear or hysteretic response no instantaneous stored-energy density is defined or claimed by this item, and the general dispersive work balance is not supplied. The identities hold only where the fields and sources have the stated regularity, the fixed-volume form keeps its boundary term, and no conservation of $\int_{\Omega'}u$ is asserted unless that term vanishes. No empirical claim is made.
items.strategy: **Proof technique:** dot the macroscopic curl equations with the complementary fields and use the cross-product divergence identity. (a): by [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]], $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$. Taking the Euclidean inner product ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) of the first with $E$ and of the second with $H$ gives $E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H=E\cdot J_f+E\cdot\partial_tD$ and $H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E=-H\cdot\partial_tB$. By [[lem-the-divergence-and-curl-of-a-cross-product]], $\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E-E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H$; subtracting the two scalar equations from this identity gives $\operatorname{div}S+\partial_t\bigl(\tfrac12E\cdot D+\tfrac12B\cdot H\bigr)+J_f\cdot E=0$, because the symmetry of $\varepsilon$ gives $E\cdot\partial_tD=\tfrac12\partial_t(E\cdot\varepsilon E)$ and the symmetry of $\mu$ gives $H\cdot\partial_tB=\tfrac12\partial_t(H\cdot\mu H)$, using $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the product rule of [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. Positivity is positive definiteness of $\varepsilon,\mu$: $u$ is a sum of two nonnegative quadratic forms, vanishing only when $E=H=0$. (b): $J_f\cdot E=E\cdot\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E$ and $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ for symmetric positive semidefinite $\sigma$. (c): [[lem-em-parameter-integrals]] differentiates $t\mapsto\int_{\Omega'}u$ under the integral sign and [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-piecewise-c-one-domains]] converts $\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S$ into the boundary flux; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is exactly the hypothesis of that divergence theorem and is used only in this clause. (d) records the restrictions. No constitutive assumption beyond the declared closure branch, and no empirical premise, is used.

items.title: Curves, regular causal curves and future timelike worldlines in affine Minkowski space
items.statement: Let (A,V,eta,C^+) be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space (def-sr-affine-minkowski-model) and let I be an order-convex subset of R with at least two elements (def-interval); a curve of the model is a map x: I -> A. (a) Derivative and regularity of the parametrization. For s in I and h nonzero with s + h in I the difference quotient (x(s+h) - x(s))/h is an element of V, the displacement from x(s) to x(s+h) divided by the real number h; the curve is differentiable at s when the limit of these quotients as h -> 0 exists in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, and then this limit, written x'(s) in V, is the tangent vector of x at s. If x_A: A -> R^4 is the chart of an inertial frame (def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart), then x is differentiable at s exactly when the R^4-valued map x_A o x is differentiable at s in the sense of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral, and then x'(s) = E((x_A o x)'(s)), where E: R^4 -> V is the frame isomorphism; this does not depend on the inertial chart used, because inertial chart transitions are affine, hence smooth (lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas), and all norms on the finite-dimensional V give the same limit. The curve is C^1 when it is differentiable at every point of I and the derivative map s |-> x'(s), I -> V, is continuous (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity); it is C^k for k >= 1 when x' is C^{k-1}. A curve on a compact interval [a,b] contained in I is piecewise C^1 when there is a finite partition a = s_0 < s_1 < ... < s_m = b such that x is C^1 on every open subinterval (s_{i-1},s_i) and the finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in V. These are limits of (x(t+h)-x(t))/h over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions that x'(s) has a limit as s approaches a corner. Their finiteness implies continuity of x at the corners. No continuous extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints of I are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over I. (b) Causal character. Let x be differentiable at s in I. Then x is regular at s if x'(s) is not the zero vector; x is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) at s if the vector x'(s) is timelike (respectively null, spacelike, causal) in the sense of def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors, and x is future-directed at s if x'(s) is future timelike or future null in the sense of def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets. The zero vector has no causal character, so only a regular curve has a causal character at s. (c) Worldlines. A future timelike worldline (massive worldline) is a C^1 curve x: I -> A with x'(s) future timelike for every s in I; a future causal curve (respectively a future null curve) is a C^1 curve with x'(s) future causal (respectively future null) for every s in I. A piecewise C^1 worldline is a piecewise C^1 curve whose tangents at every point of each open smooth piece and whose finite one-sided difference-quotient tangents at both endpoints of every piece are future timelike, and a C^k worldline is a worldline whose parametrization is C^k; C^2 regularity is what makes the four-acceleration of this page available. The parametrization is part of the curve: the image of a future timelike worldline is also the image of the past-directed curve s |-> x(-s), which is not a worldline of this model, and no worldline or clock claim is attached to it. The definition asserts the existence of no worldline beyond those given by an explicit formula.
items.strategy: A definition item: it fixes the curve, regularity and causal-character language on which the page's items rest, and makes no proof claim beyond well-definedness. Obligations: (i) the difference quotient is an element of V because the affine action gives a displacement for every ordered pair of events, and the limit is taken in the finite-dimensional real vector space V, so no norm has to be chosen; (ii) the identification with the coordinate calculus and the independence of x'(s) and of C^k from the inertial chart are justified by the affine, hence smooth, chart transitions of lem-affine-minkowski-charts-form-a-smooth-atlas, with the published vector-valued derivative of def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral as the coordinate calculus; (iii) continuity of x' is continuity of a V-valued map (def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity), and one-sided derivatives at endpoints are limits over the domain I as in def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral; (iv) causal character and the future/past alternative are those of the model's vector classification and time orientation, with the zero vector excluded, so regularity is implicit in every causal character; (v) null and spacelike curves are distinguished from massive worldlines and are used later only to delimit the proper-time construction. No choice principle is used: all objects are finite-dimensional or explicitly parametrized. In the piecewise clause, a finite one-sided quotient derivative v gives x(t+h)-x(t)=h(v+o(1)), proving one-sided endpoint continuity directly. It does not imply convergence of the interior derivative; no such hypothesis is added. The timelike condition applies at every smooth point and to each side of a corner, and excludes zero tangents.

items.title: Improper integrability and endpoint increments of weak piecewise future causal curves
items.statement: Let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 curve in the sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline, with a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, C^1 on each open piece and finite one-sided difference-quotient derivatives at both ends of each piece. Assume its tangents are nonzero future causal at every open-piece point and at each one-sided endpoint. In any inertial chart write y=(y^0,z), z in R^3. On a piece (alpha,beta), choose r in (alpha,beta); for a function g continuous there, write integral_(alpha,beta) g for lim_(u downarrow alpha) integral_u^r g + lim_(v uparrow beta) integral_r^v g when both limits are finite. Then: (a) y is continuous on [alpha,beta], y^{0'}>=|z'|>=0 on (alpha,beta), and y^{0'}>0 there. (b) Every coordinate derivative is absolutely improperly Riemann integrable; its signed improper integral equals the corresponding endpoint increment. The continuous functions |z'| and f=sqrt((y^{0'})^2-|z'|^2)=sqrt(-eta(x',x')) have finite nonnegative improper integrals, with integral f<=integral y^{0'}=y^0(beta)-y^0(alpha). (c) The improper values are independent of r, additive under subdivision, and the finite piece sums are independent of the admissible partition. (d) D=x(b)-x(a) is nonzero future causal: D^0>0 and |D_spatial|<=D^0 in every inertial chart. If some interior or one-sided endpoint tangent is future timelike, D is future timelike. Coordinate time is strictly increasing on every nondegenerate subinterval. The integrals need not be ordinary closed-piece Riemann integrals. No derivative-limit hypothesis, Lebesgue-integration premise, clock identification, or choice principle is used.
items.strategy: Complete local adaptation of the flat future-cone integral argument, with endpoint integrability supplied rather than assumed. (a) Finite quotient derivative v at an endpoint gives x(t+h)-x(t)=h(v+o(1)), hence endpoint continuity; C1 gives interior continuity. The future cone coordinate criterion gives y0'>=|z'| and y0'>0 on each open piece. The square root is continuous on nonnegative reals: positive arguments use thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives with exponent 1/2; at zero, 0<=t<epsilon^2 implies 0<=sqrt(t)<epsilon. Thus the spatial norm and causal density are continuous even at a null tangent or a zero spatial component. Since y0'>=|z'|>=0, their squared values lie between 0 and (y0')^2, giving 0<=f<=y0' by the nonnegative square-root order. (b) On every alpha<u<v<beta, the derivative is continuous on [u,v], so thm-continuous-implies-integrable and thm-ftc-second-part give integral_u^v yj'=yj(v)-yj(u). Fix r inside. For y0' the left and right limits are y0(r)-y0(alpha) and y0(beta)-y0(r), finite by endpoint continuity and nonnegative. For any continuous 0<=g<=y0', the left truncation integrals are increasing as u decreases, bounded above by y0(r)-y0(alpha); completeness supplies their supremum S. Given epsilon>0 choose u* with integral_u*^r g>S-epsilon; every alpha<u<u* then has integral_u^r g between S-epsilon and S, proving the limit S. The right side is identical. Apply this to |yj'|, |z'| and f; all are continuous inside and bounded above by y0'. Signed coordinate integrals converge by the truncated FTC and endpoint continuity; thus each derivative is absolutely improperly integrable and has the exact endpoint increment. (c) Ordinary integral additivity on truncations and finite limits show independence of r and additivity under each interior cut. Any two admissible finite partitions have a common refinement, so all finite sums agree. (d) On truncations, the vector-integral norm inequality gives |z(v)-z(u)|<=integral_u^v |z'|<=integral_u^v y0'. Pass to endpoints and sum with the Euclidean triangle inequality to obtain |D_spatial|<=D0. Positive y0' on a compact interior interval gives a positive time increment, and nonnegativity on the rest gives D0>0; apply the same argument to any nondegenerate restriction for strict time monotonicity. At an interior timelike tangent, y0'-|z'| is continuous and positive in a compact interior neighborhood, so its integral is positive and the inequality becomes strict. At a left endpoint with timelike one-sided quotient v, (y(alpha+h)-y(alpha))/h tends to v, so for some h>0 that quotient is future timelike by openness of the cone. This subdisplacement is future timelike, and the remaining subdisplacement is future causal by the already proved non-strict inequality; adding their coordinates yields a future timelike sum. At a right endpoint use (y(beta)-y(beta-h))/h similarly. At a corner use the corresponding adjacent piece. This proves the endpoint-only timelike clause without continuity of the derivative at the corner. No closed-piece derivative integrability or countable choice is assumed.

items.title: Proper time along a future timelike worldline
items.statement: Let c > 0 be a fixed real number (the conversion constant of the model, whose physical interpretation is supplied with the model's coordinate conventions) and let x: I -> A be a C^1 future timelike worldline (def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline). Then the function g_x: I -> R, g_x(s) := -eta(x'(s),x'(s)), is continuous and strictly positive: continuity holds because in an eta-orthonormal basis eta(x'(s),x'(s)) = sum_{a,b} eta_ab (x'(s))^a (x'(s))^b is a finite sum of products of continuous real functions (lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis, thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions), and positivity is the future timelike hypothesis (def-causal-classification-of-lorentz-vectors). Hence u |-> sqrt(g_x(u)) is continuous on I (thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives, thm-composition-of-continuous-functions) and Riemann integrable on every compact subinterval of I (thm-continuous-implies-integrable). For s_0, s in I the proper time from s_0 to s is tau(s) := c^{-1} integral_{s_0}^{s} sqrt(-eta(x'(u),x'(u))) du, the integral being the oriented integral of def-oriented-integral; explicitly, for a < b in I, tau(b) - tau(a) = c^{-1} integral_a^b sqrt(-eta(x'(u),x'(u))) du, and changing the base point s_0 changes tau by an additive constant. tau depends on the parametrized history of x and on the parameter values; its invariance under increasing C^1 reparametrizations is proved in lem-sr-proper-time-reparametrization-invariance. For the straight future timelike segment x(s) = p + (s - s_0)(q - p) one has tau(b) - tau(a) = c^{-1} sqrt(-eta(q-p,q-p)) (b - a), which is the straight-segment proper time of the model's coordinate conventions. The construction is restricted to future timelike worldlines: at a null point the integrand vanishes, for a spacelike curve -eta(x',x') is negative and the square root is not a real number, and for a past-directed timelike curve the integral is defined but is not attached to a worldline of the model.
items.strategy: Definition item with well-definedness obligations: (i) the integrand is the composition of the continuous map s |-> x'(s), the continuous quadratic form v |-> -eta(v,v) (checked in coordinates in an eta-orthonormal basis, since eta is bilinear on the finite-dimensional V) and the continuous power t |-> t^{1/2} on (0,inf); (ii) strict positivity of g_x is exactly the future timelike hypothesis, so the square root is a positive real number on all of I; (iii) existence of the integral on compact subintervals is thm-continuous-implies-integrable, and the oriented convention makes tau(s_0) = 0 and reverses the sign when the endpoints are exchanged; (iv) the base point enters only additively, so elapsed times between parameter values are intrinsic; (v) the straight-segment consistency is a direct evaluation: x' is constant on a straight segment and the integrand is c^{-1} sqrt(-eta(q-p,q-p)) times the parameter length. No choice principle is used. The item deliberately does not assert that tau is differentiable or invertible (that is lem-sr-proper-time-parametrization) nor that a physical clock reads tau (that belongs to the adopted physical interpretation).

items.title: Total proper time of a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline
items.statement: Let c>0 be the conversion constant of def-sr-proper-time and let x:[a,b]->A, a<b, be a piecewise C^1 future timelike worldline in the weak sense of def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline: x is C^1 on each open piece of a finite partition a=s_0<...<s_m=b, its interior tangents and finite one-sided difference-quotient endpoint tangents are future timelike, and continuous extension of the derivative is not assumed. (i) On each open piece let g_i(t)=sqrt(-eta(x'(t),x'(t)))>0. Define its two-ended improper Riemann integral by the convention of lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability. That lemma proves each value finite and nonnegative; it is positive since g_i is positive and continuous on a compact interior subinterval. (ii) Define total proper time by Delta tau_[a,b](x)=c^{-1} sum_i integral_(s_(i-1),s_i) g_i. The finite sum is independent of the partition, by subdivision additivity and a common refinement. It is independent of the inertial chart because eta and the tangent are chart independent; constant Lorentz changes preserve the density already on each proper truncation. (iii) Choose a proper-time basepoint t_0 in [a,b], independently of the partition label s_0=a. Define tau_x(s)=Delta tau_[t_0,s](x) for s>=t_0, and tau_x(s)=-Delta tau_[s,t_0](x) for s<t_0, with tau_x(t_0)=0, using restrictions and oriented limits. It is strictly increasing, and changing t_0 changes only an additive constant. (iv) Corner hypothesis (H) is the special case in which each open-piece derivative has finite limits at both ends and thus extends continuously to the closed piece. Those limits equal the one-sided quotient derivatives. Under (H), each g_i extends continuously and positively to the closed piece, its improper integral equals its ordinary Riemann integral there, and the same finite-sum formula applies. In particular if x is globally C^1 on [a,b], Delta tau(x)=tau(b)-tau(a) of def-sr-proper-time. (v) Delta tau(x)>0. If on piece i the tangent is a constant future timelike vector d_i, the contribution is c^{-1}(s_i-s_(i-1))sqrt(-eta(d_i,d_i)); this gives the finite sum of straight-segment proper times. (vi) Additivity over concatenation: for a<b<d, restrictions of a weak piecewise worldline x on [a,d] satisfy Delta tau_[a,d](x)=Delta tau_[a,b](x)+Delta tau_[b,d](x). Insert b in the partition and use (ii). The definition supplies metric time only; identification with an ideal clock reading is the separate physical clock postulate. No global C^1 inverse, tangent at a kink, or four-acceleration at a kink is asserted.
items.strategy: Well-definedness is lem-sr-weak-piecewise-causal-integrability: endpoint continuity, finite improper integrals dominated in an inertial chart by the nonnegative time derivative, truncated FTC and partition independence. Strict positivity follows by a compact interior neighborhood on which g_i is positive and continuous. Refinements split each integral, and a common refinement gives independence of the finite partition. Restriction/additivity also give the based function, strict increase and base-point constants. Under (H), if the extended derivative is f_i, truncated FTC gives x(v)-x(u)=integral_u^v f_i. Passing u to the endpoint shows that the one-sided difference quotient is the average of f_i over a shrinking interval and therefore tends to its continuous endpoint value; thus the extension equals the finite quotient tangent. The extended density is continuous and strictly positive on the compact closed piece. Its bounded omitted endpoint tails tend to zero, so its improper value equals the ordinary Riemann value. Global C1 is the one-piece (H) case and agrees with def-sr-proper-time. Constant tangents give the displayed straight-segment calculation directly. All steps are finite-dimensional one-variable real analysis and use no choice principle; no physical premise supplies mathematical integrability.
